entry.title: Beyond Data Silos: Powering the Autonomous Enterprise with SAP's Next-Generation Data Fabric and AI
entry.content:
The next era of enterprise transformation is not just about making data available. It is about making data intelligent, contextual, trusted, and actionable.

Artificial Intelligence is rapidly transforming how businesses operate. From demand forecasting and supply chain optimization to financial planning and customer engagement, AI agents are moving beyond generating insights to actively supporting business decisions and executing complex workflows.

But there is one fundamental challenge: AI is only as intelligent as the business context it understands.

Enterprise data is often scattered across applications, databases, data warehouses, and cloud platforms. Even when organizations have access to vast amounts of information, disconnected systems, inconsistent master data, and fragmented business definitions make it difficult for AI to understand how the business actually operates.

At SAP TechEd Berlin 2026, SAP introduced a new wave of innovations in SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) to address this challenge and accelerate the journey toward the autonomous enterprise.

With advancements in open lakehouse architecture, zero-copy data sharing, enterprise master data management, and business knowledge modeling, SAP is taking an important step toward creating an intelligent data foundation where AI agents can understand business operations, make informed decisions, and act with greater autonomy and confidence.

Let's explore the innovations shaping this transformation.

1. Breaking Data Silos: An Open Lakehouse Built for the AI Era

Enterprise data should not be restricted by platforms, storage locations, or technology boundaries. However, traditional data architectures often require organizations to replicate information across multiple systems, creating additional costs, operational complexity, and inconsistent data.

SAP is addressing this challenge by strengthening its open lakehouse foundation through the completed acquisition of Dremio.

The vision is simple: make enterprise data accessible wherever it resides, without constantly moving or duplicating it.

Key innovations include:

  • Open lakehouse architecture: Native Apache Iceberg support and a universal catalog powered by Apache Polaris provide an open foundation for discovering, governing, and sharing enterprise data.

  • Zero-copy data sharing: SAP BDC Connect enables interoperability with platforms such as Databricks, Snowflake, Google Cloud, AWS, and Microsoft, minimizing unnecessary data duplication.

  • Federated data access: Powered by Dremio's high-performance SQL query engine, organizations can query distributed data across SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, and PostgreSQL without physically moving it.

  • Autonomous query optimization: Dremio Reflections intelligently optimize query performance by learning workload patterns and automatically precomputing frequently accessed results.

An especially exciting development is the integration with Joule Work, allowing business users to ask complex questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in trusted enterprise data.

The business impact: Less time managing data pipelines, fewer data silos, faster analytics, and a scalable data foundation for AI agents operating across enterprise environments.

2. SAP and Databricks: Accelerating the Next Generation of Data and AI Innovation

 

The future of enterprise AI requires collaboration between business applications, data engineering platforms, and advanced AI technologies.

SAP's expanded partnership with Databricks brings additional industry-leading capabilities into SAP Databricks within SAP Business Data Cloud.

The expanded capabilities include:

  • Lakeflow

  • Agent Bricks

  • Unity Gateway

  • Lakebase

Through SAP Application Data Foundation, organizations can access SAP application data directly within their preferred SAP BDC engine, including SAP Databricks.

This creates an opportunity to combine the rich business semantics of SAP data with the advanced analytics and AI capabilities of Databricks.

Consider a real-world manufacturing scenario.

A manufacturer wants to predict future product demand, optimize inventory, and improve supply chain efficiency.

Traditionally, this could involve extracting historical sales data, integrating inventory information, combining external market intelligence, and building complex data pipelines before developing forecasting models.

With SAP Business Data Cloud and SAP Databricks, data professionals can access SAP data, enrich it with third-party information, and create custom data products on a semantically rich foundation.

AI models can then generate forecasts that are aligned with the business logic and relationships already embedded in SAP systems.

The business impact: Accelerated AI development, reduced integration complexity, lower total cost of ownership, and faster realization of business value from cloud transformation.

3. SAP Reltio: Turning Fragmented Master Data into a Trusted 360-Degree Business View

 

One of the biggest barriers to enterprise AI adoption is inconsistent master data.

Imagine an organization where the same customer exists in multiple systems with different customer IDs, addresses, names, and transaction histories.

A human employee might recognize that these records represent the same customer. But an AI agent needs reliable entity resolution and connected business relationships to reach the same conclusion.

This is where SAP Reltio becomes important.

Following the completion of its acquisition, SAP Reltio is now generally available within SAP Business Data Cloud, bringing multi-domain Master Data Management (MDM) capabilities natively into the business data fabric.

Its AI-based entity resolution capabilities help organizations:

  • Identify and reconcile duplicate records across SAP and non-SAP systems.

  • Harmonize inconsistent customer, supplier, and product information.

  • Build unified 360-degree views of critical business entities.

  • Connect business attributes, relationships, and interactions.

  • Publish trusted entity profiles as governed data products.

The significance goes beyond traditional master data management.

When Joule and Joule Agents access unified business entity profiles, they gain a more complete understanding of customers, suppliers, products, and their relationships across the enterprise.

For example, a customer service agent can potentially understand a customer's purchase history, outstanding invoices, service interactions, and business relationships through connected and trusted information.

The business impact: Better data quality, improved decision-making, stronger customer intelligence, and a reliable foundation for context-aware enterprise AI.

4. SAP Knowledge Graph and Ontology Manager: Giving AI Agents the Context to Think and Act

 

This is arguably one of the most important developments in SAP's journey toward the autonomous enterprise.

AI agents do not simply need access to information. They need to understand what that information represents, how different business entities are connected, and which business rules govern their decisions.

For example, knowing that an invoice is overdue is useful. But understanding the customer associated with that invoice, the agreed payment terms, the credit exposure, and the organization's collections policies is what enables meaningful business action.

SAP Knowledge Graph provides this connected business understanding by linking enterprise entities, relationships, and business rules.

At SAP TechEd Berlin 2026, SAP introduced SAP Business Data Cloud Ontology Manager, an AI-assisted experience that enables organizations to create domain-specific views of SAP Knowledge Graph.

Rather than exposing an entire enterprise knowledge model to every AI agent, organizations can create curated views containing only the information relevant to a particular business scenario.

Consider a collections AI agent.

To support collections operations effectively, the agent needs to understand:

  • Customer relationships.

  • Outstanding invoices.

  • Payment terms.

  • Credit risk.

  • Financial transactions.

  • Relevant business rules and policies.

Using Ontology Manager, organizations can create a dedicated collections domain view that connects these entities and relationships.

Joule Agents can then use this context to generate more relevant answers, recommendations, and business actions.

Even more importantly, these domain-specific views inherit business definitions and governance from SAP Knowledge Graph.

This means organizations can reuse the same business semantics across collections, cash flow management, order management, and other business scenarios without repeatedly redefining the underlying concepts.

The business impact: More intelligent AI agents, consistent business semantics, reusable enterprise knowledge, and decisions grounded in how the organization actually operates.

5. The Bigger Picture: SAP Is Moving Beyond Data Management Toward Business Intelligence for Autonomous Operations

The real significance of these announcements is not any individual technology or product integration. It is how these capabilities come together to create a unified foundation for enterprise intelligence.

Consider how the different innovations complement each other:

SAPinnovationRoleintheautonomousenterprise

Dremio Open Lakehouse

Makes distributed enterprise data accessible

Apache Iceberg and Polaris

Enables open data management and discovery

SAP BDC Connect

Supports zero-copy data sharing

SAP Databricks

Accelerates advanced analytics and AI development

SAP Reltio

Establishes trusted, unified business entities

SAP Knowledge Graph

Connects enterprise data with business meaning

Ontology Manager

Creates reusable, domain-specific business context

Joule and Joule Agents

Turn business context into intelligent assistance and action

 

Together, these capabilities establish a powerful foundation for the next generation of enterprise AI.

The transformation can be understood through four interconnected layers:

The foundation of an autonomous enterprise

AI & Autonomous Actions

Joule · Joule Agents · Intelligent business workflows

 

Business Context & Semantics

SAP Knowledge Graph · Ontology Manager · SAP Reltio

 

Data Integration & Interoperability

SAP BDC Connect · Zero-copy sharing · SAP Databricks

 

Open Data Foundation

Dremio · Apache Iceberg · Apache Polaris · Distributed data sources

Conceptual representation of how the announced capabilities work together, not an official SAP reference architecture.

This approach shifts the enterprise data strategy from simply collecting and processing information to creating a connected business intelligence ecosystem.

6. What Enterprises Should Take Away from These Announcements

For business leaders, enterprise architects, data engineers, and AI transformation teams, these innovations highlight several important priorities:

1. Think beyond traditional data integration. Build open architectures that allow data to remain accessible across platforms without unnecessary duplication.

2. Treat business context as a strategic asset. High-quality data alone is not enough. Business definitions, relationships, policies, and semantics must also be available to AI.

3. Invest in trusted master data. AI-driven decisions require consistent customer, supplier, product, and financial information across systems.

4. Make enterprise knowledge reusable. Domain-specific ontologies can help organizations develop AI agents that understand individual business processes without rebuilding business semantics for every use case.

5. Move from AI experimentation to business execution. The ultimate objective is to enable AI agents to support real business workflows with the appropriate governance, context, and controls.

Conclusion: The Future Belongs to Enterprises That Connect Data, Context, and Intelligence

SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 marks an important milestone in SAP's vision for the autonomous enterprise.

With the evolution of SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP is bringing together open lakehouse architecture, cross-platform data interoperability, advanced analytics, unified master data, enterprise knowledge graphs, and AI-powered business agents.

The bigger opportunity is not simply to make enterprise data available to AI. It is to make enterprise data understandable and actionable.

Imagine an enterprise where AI agents can understand customer relationships, recognize supply chain dependencies, interpret financial policies, evaluate business risks, and recommend or execute actions based on trusted organizational knowledge.

That is the direction SAP Business Data Cloud is helping organizations move toward.

The next competitive advantage will not come from having more data or deploying more AI models. It will come from connecting data with business meaning and enabling intelligent systems to turn that understanding into action.

The autonomous enterprise is no longer just a vision of the future. With trusted data, connected business context, and intelligent AI agents, organizations are beginning to build its foundation today.

 

Reference

Original SAP Announcement: Advancing SAP Lakehouse and New Data Fabric Innovations in SAP Business Data Cloud for the Autonomous Enterprise

entry.title: From CDS to A2A: Building a Production CAP Agent with @cap-js/agents and SAP AI Core
entry.content:
From CDS to A2A: Building a Production CAP Agent with @cap-js/agents and SAP AI Core

 

The @cap-js/agents package (CAP v10 / cds-dk 10.x) introduces a surprisingly small surface area for a very large capability: annotate one CDS service with @AGent, define your tools as CDS actions, drop Markdown skill files into a skills/ folder, and your CAP service is instantly an A2A-compatible AI agent that SAP Joule or any orchestrator can discover and drive.

This post documents a full production implementation: seven agent tools, native Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) using the @AGent.hitl annotation, multi-modal PDF extraction via Claude Sonnet 4 on SAP AI Core, three skills files grounding LLM behaviour per workflow phase, and a SAPUI5 chat frontend that speaks directly to the A2A endpoint. All in a single MTA deployed to BTP Cloud Foundry.

Contents

  1. Architecture overview
  2. Defining the agent service in CDS — 7 tools
  3. Native HITL with @agent.hitl
  4. TypeScript handler — delegating to existing services
  5. Skill files — grounding per workflow phase
  6. AI-driven template matching
  7. SAP AI Core — LLM binding and multi-modal extraction
  8. SAPUI5 chat frontend — A2A client integration
  9. Security — XSUAA scopes
  10. MTA build & deploy
  11. SAP Build Work Zone
  12. Key decisions and lessons learned

1. Architecture Overview

The entire agent capability lives in two places: srv/agent/service.cds + srv/agent/service.ts on the backend, and app/agent-ui/ for the SAPUI5 chat frontend. There is no dedicated orchestrator service — the @AGentannotation handles the A2A message loop, and the agent handler delegates to two existing CAP services via cds.connect.to().

 

Layer Component Role

FrontendSAPUI5 chat app (app/agent-ui/)Phase state machine (UPLOAD → CHAT → SUBMITTED). Sends PDF + text to A2A endpoint. Renders agent responses as chat bubbles. Handles HITL approval dialog.
AgentWorkflowAgentService — @AGentExposes 7 tools to the LLM. The framework drives the multi-turn message loop; the handler only implements what each tool does.
Core servicesDocumentService, TemplateServiceExisting OData V4 CAP services. The agent calls them in-process via cds.connect.to() using a privileged user to bypass UI auth checks.
AISAP AI Core — Claude Sonnet 4Both the agent framework (tool selection) and service handlers (extraction, template generation) call AI Core via the llm CDS binding.
ERPERP on-premise via BTP DestinationDocumentService.submitToERP() sends a $batch PATCH over Cloud Connector.
DataSAP HANA Cloud (HDI)Stores DocumentJob, ExtractedHeader, ExtractedLineItem, ExtractionTemplate.

2. Defining the Agent Service in CDS — 7 Tools

The CDS service definition is where you define what the LLM can do. Every action becomes a tool. The @Common.Label annotation is the tool description the LLM sees when deciding which tool to call.

// srv/agent/service.cds

@path : '/odata/v4/workflowagent'
@agent                              // exposes A2A endpoint + agent card
service WorkflowAgentService {

  // Tool 1 — match uploaded document against active templates.
  // If no match: auto-create a DRAFT template, run test extraction,
  // return needsActivation=true so agent can ask user before activating.
  @(Common.Label: 'Match or Create Extraction Template')
  action matchOrCreateTemplate(
    content  : LargeBinary @(Core.MediaType: 'application/octet-stream'),
    fileName : String(255),
    mimeType : String(100)
  ) returns {
    templateId       : UUID;
    templateName     : String(100);
    matched          : Boolean;
    needsActivation  : Boolean;
    testItemCount    : Integer;
    testFlaggedCount : Integer;
    testConfidence   : Decimal(5,2);
    message          : String(500);
  };

  // Tool 2 — start async AI extraction.
  // Returns immediately with jobId. Agent polls Tool 3 until READY.
  @(Common.Label: 'Upload Document and Start Extraction')
  action uploadAndExtract(
    content    : LargeBinary @(Core.MediaType: 'application/octet-stream'),
    fileName   : String(255),
    mimeType   : String(100),
    templateId : UUID
  ) returns {
    jobId   : UUID;
    status  : String(20);
    message : String(500);
  };

  // Tool 3 — poll extraction status + confidence summary.
  @(Common.Label: 'Get Extraction Status')
  action getExtractionStatus(jobId : UUID) returns {
    status        : String(20);
    fileName      : String(255);
    totalItems    : Integer;
    flaggedItems  : Integer;    // items with confidence < 70%
    avgConfidence : Decimal(5,2);
    errorMessage  : String(1000);
  };

  // Tool 4 — return full extraction: header + all line items with confidence.
  // Agent formats this as a markdown table for the user.
  @(Common.Label: 'Review Extraction Results')
  action reviewExtraction(jobId : UUID) returns {
    jobId        : UUID;
    docRef1      : String(4);    // e.g. warehouse code
    docRef2      : String(20);   // e.g. document number
    docRef3      : String(4);    // e.g. fiscal year
    totalItems   : Integer;
    flaggedItems : Integer;
    items        : array of {
      itemNo     : String(10);
      itemKey    : String(40);   // e.g. barcode / HU
      quantity   : Integer;
      unit       : String(3);
      confidence : Decimal(5,2);
      flagged    : Boolean;
    };
  };

  // Tool 5 — conversational corrections, re-extract, refine template, re-read.
  // Special message prefixes:
  //   __REEXTRACT__:<hint>   re-extract the full document
  //   __REFINE__:<hint>      refine the template extraction prompt
  //   __REREAD__:<items>    re-read specific items from the original scan
  //   __SAVE_TEMPLATE__:<n> persist corrections back to the template
  @(Common.Label: 'Chat About Extraction')
  action chatAboutExtraction(
    jobId   : UUID,
    message : String(2000)
  ) returns {
    reply        : String(4000);
    type         : String(20);  // 'text' | 'field_update'
    updatedItems : array of {
      itemNo       : String(10);
      itemKey      : String(40);
      quantity     : Integer;
      unit         : String(3);
      confidence   : Decimal(5,2);
    };
  };

  // Tool 6 — submit to ERP.
  // @agent.hitl: the A2A task pauses in "input-required" state.
  // The handler ONLY runs after the user clicks Confirm in the frontend.
  // No manual confirmed=true flag needed — the framework handles it.
  @agent.hitl
  @(Common.Label: 'Submit to ERP')
  action submitToERP(jobId : UUID) returns {
    success : Boolean;
    message : String(500);
  };

  // Tool 7 — activate a DRAFT template created by Tool 1.
  @(Common.Label: 'Activate Extraction Template')
  action activateTemplate(templateId : UUID) returns {
    success : Boolean;
    message : String(500);
  };
}
@AGent.hitl vs. manual confirmed flag: The @AGent.hitl annotation on submitToERP is the framework-native way to pause the A2A task and wait for human approval. It differs from the manual confirmed=false / confirmed=true two-call pattern in that the task state machine handles the pause automatically — no extra action parameter needed, and the handler code runs once, after approval, with no conditional branch.

3. Native HITL with @AGent.hitl

When the LLM calls an action annotated with @AGent.hitl, the @cap-js/agents framework:

  1. Transitions the A2A task to input-required state
  2. Returns the pre-submission summary to the frontend as the agent message
  3. Waits — the handler does not execute yet
  4. When the user clicks Confirm in the frontend, the task resumes
  5. Only now does the action handler execute and the ERP write happen
// The annotation in CDS is the entire HITL configuration:
@agent.hitl
@(Common.Label: 'Submit to ERP')
action submitToERP(jobId : UUID) returns { success : Boolean; message : String(500); };

// The handler is called exactly ONCE, after user approval.
// No guard condition needed:
this.on('submitToERP', async (req: Request) => {
  const { jobId } = req.data;
  const docSvc = await cds.connect.to('DocumentService');

  const result = await (docSvc as any)
    .tx({ user: new cds.User.Privileged() })
    .send('submitToERP', { jobId });

  return { success: result?.success ?? false, message: result?.message ?? '' };
});

The frontend needs to detect the input-required state and render an approval dialog. In the SAPUI5 controller, the A2A polling loop checks the task status and reacts accordingly:

// app/agent-ui/webapp/controller/Main.controller.js (simplified)
var A2A_BASE = "/odata/v4/workflowagent";

// Send a message to the A2A endpoint
_sendMessage: async function(text, fileData) {
  var payload = { message: text };
  if (fileData) payload.data = fileData;  // { content, fileName, mimeType }

  // If a HITL task is awaiting confirmation, send the approval
  if (this._taskId) {
    await fetch(A2A_BASE + "/tasks/" + this._taskId + "/resume", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ approved: true })
    });
    this._taskId = null;
    return;
  }

  // New message turn — create or continue the A2A context
  var url = this._contextId
    ? A2A_BASE + "/contexts/" + this._contextId + "/messages"
    : A2A_BASE + "/messages";

  var resp = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload)
  });
  var body = await resp.json();

  this._contextId = body.contextId;   // persist for next turn

  if (body.status === "input-required") {
    // HITL pause: save taskId, render approval dialog
    this._taskId = body.taskId;
    this._renderHITLCard(body.message);
    return;
  }

  this._renderAgentMessage(body.message);
},
Context ID vs. Task ID: The A2A context ID persists across the entire conversation — it gives the agent its full history. The task ID is only set when the task is paused in input-required (HITL) state. Clear the task ID after resume so subsequent messages create new tasks within the same context.

4. TypeScript Handler — Delegating to Existing Services

The agent handler does not reimplement any business logic. Every tool delegates to the existing DocumentService or TemplateService using cds.connect.to() with a privileged transaction, so service-level authorisation checks are bypassed (the agent itself enforces role checks via XSUAA).

// srv/agent/service.ts  (key patterns)
import cds from '@sap/cds';
import type { Request } from '@sap/cds';

class WorkflowAgentServiceHandler extends cds.ApplicationService {

  async init(): Promise<void> {

    // Tool 2: uploadAndExtract — delegates entirely to DocumentService
    this.on('uploadAndExtract', async (req: Request) => {
      const { content, fileName, mimeType, templateId } = req.data;
      const docSvc = await cds.connect.to('DocumentService');

      const buf = Buffer.isBuffer(content)
        ? content
        : Buffer.from(content as string, 'base64');

      const result = await (docSvc as any)
        .tx({ user: new cds.User.Privileged() })  // bypass UI auth on inner service
        .send('processDocument', { content: buf, fileName, mimeType, templateId });

      return {
        jobId  : result?.ID,
        status : result?.status ?? 'UPLOADING',
        message: `Extraction started for "${fileName}". Polling status...`,
      };
    });

    // Tool 3: getExtractionStatus — direct HANA read
    this.on('getExtractionStatus', async (req: Request) => {
      const { DocumentJob, ExtractedHeader, ExtractedLineItem } =
        cds.entities('com.example.docai');
      const job   = await SELECT.one.from(DocumentJob).where({ ID: req.data.jobId });
      const hdr   = await SELECT.one.from(ExtractedHeader).where({ job_ID: req.data.jobId });
      let total = 0, flagged = 0, avg = 0;

      if (hdr) {
        const items = await SELECT.from(ExtractedLineItem).where({ header_ID: hdr.ID });
        total   = items.length;
        flagged = items.filter((i: any) => Number(i.confidence) < 70).length;
        const scores = items.map((i: any) => Number(i.confidence)).filter(Number.isFinite);
        avg = scores.length ? Math.round(scores.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / scores.length * 100) / 100 : 0;
      }

      return { status: job?.status, fileName: job?.fileName,
               totalItems: total, flaggedItems: flagged,
               avgConfidence: avg, errorMessage: job?.errorMessage ?? '' };
    });

    // Tool 4: reviewExtraction — returns full structured result
    this.on('reviewExtraction', async (req: Request) => {
      const { ExtractedHeader, ExtractedLineItem } = cds.entities('com.example.docai');
      const hdr   = await SELECT.one.from(ExtractedHeader).where({ job_ID: req.data.jobId });
      if (!hdr) return req.error(404, `No document found for job ${req.data.jobId}`);
      const items = await SELECT.from(ExtractedLineItem).where({ header_ID: hdr.ID });
      const flaggedCount = items.filter((i: any) => Number(i.confidence) < 70).length;

      return {
        jobId      : req.data.jobId,
        docRef1    : hdr.field1 ?? '',
        docRef2    : hdr.referenceId ?? '',
        docRef3    : hdr.field2 ?? '',
        totalItems : items.length,
        flaggedItems: flaggedCount,
        items: items.map((i: any) => ({
          itemNo    : i.itemNo ?? '',
          itemKey   : i.itemCode ?? '',
          quantity  : i.quantity ?? 0,
          unit      : i.unitOfMeasure ?? '',
          confidence: i.confidence ?? null,
          flagged   : Number(i.confidence) < 70,
        })),
      };
    });

    // Tool 5: chatAboutExtraction — delegates to DocumentService.chatWithDocument
    this.on('chatAboutExtraction', async (req: Request) => {
      const { jobId, message } = req.data;
      const docSvc = await cds.connect.to('DocumentService');
      const result = await (docSvc as any)
        .tx({ user: new cds.User.Privileged() })
        .send('chatWithDocument', { jobId, message });

      return { reply: result?.reply ?? '', type: result?.type ?? 'text',
               updatedItems: result?.updatedItems ?? [] };
    });

    // Tool 6: submitToERP — handler runs only after @agent.hitl approval
    this.on('submitToERP', async (req: Request) => {
      const docSvc = await cds.connect.to('DocumentService');
      const result = await (docSvc as any)
        .tx({ user: new cds.User.Privileged() })
        .send('submitToERP', { jobId: req.data.jobId });
      return { success: result?.success ?? false, message: result?.message ?? '' };
    });

    // Tool 7: activateTemplate — delegates to TemplateService
    this.on('activateTemplate', async (req: Request) => {
      const tmplSvc = await cds.connect.to('TemplateService');
      const result  = await (tmplSvc as any)
        .tx({ user: new cds.User.Privileged() })
        .send('activateTemplate', { templateId: req.data.templateId });
      return { success: result?.success ?? false, message: result?.message ?? '' };
    });

    return super.init();
  }
}
Why cds.User.Privileged()? The outer agent service enforces XSUAA role checks (PhysInvUser / PhysInvAdmin). When it delegates internally to another CAP service, wrapping the transaction in new cds.User.Privileged() lets the inner service skip its own UI-layer checks — preventing a double-auth problem while keeping the outer gate intact.

6. AI-Driven Template Matching

Different document form layouts require tailored extraction prompts. Rather than relying on filename matching or user selection, the agent uses Claude to compare the uploaded document's visual layout against stored layout fingerprints of all active templates.

// srv/agent/service.ts — _findMatchingTemplate (private method)

private async _findMatchingTemplate(b64: string, mimeType: string) {
  const { ExtractionTemplate } = cds.entities('com.example.docai');
  const templates = await SELECT.from(ExtractionTemplate)
    .columns('ID', 'name', 'layoutFingerprint')
    .where({ status: 'ACTIVE' });

  const candidates = templates.filter((t: any) => t.layoutFingerprint);
  if (!candidates.length) return {};

  const ai = AIClient.getInstance();

  const uploadedBlock: ContentBlock = mimeType === 'application/pdf'
    ? { type: 'document', source: { type: 'base64', media_type: 'application/pdf', data: b64 } }
    : { type: 'image',    source: { type: 'base64', media_type: mimeType, data: b64 } };

  for (const tmpl of candidates) {
    const prompt = `You are comparing document layouts.

Known template layout ("${tmpl.name}"):
${tmpl.layoutFingerprint}

Does the uploaded document match this layout? Focus on:
column arrangement, field labels, table structure, header layout.
Ignore differences in actual data values.

Reply with ONLY one word: YES or NO.`;

    const { text } = await ai.invoke(
      'Compare document layouts. Reply YES or NO only.',
      [uploadedBlock, { type: 'text', text: prompt }],
    );

    if (text.trim().toUpperCase().startsWith('YES'))
      return { id: tmpl.ID, name: tmpl.name };
  }

  return {};  // no match — triggers auto-create flow
}
One AI call per template candidate. The matching loop stops at the first YES. For most deployments (a handful of active templates), this is fast enough. If you have many templates, pre-filter using a cheaper metadata heuristic (page count, aspect ratio) before calling the LLM.

</VBox>

Sending a message (with or without PDF)

// First turn: file is attached as a data part
_sendFirstMessage: async function(file) {
  var b64 = await this._fileToBase64(file);
  await this._callA2A({
    message : "Please process this document",
    data    : { content: b64, fileName: file.name, mimeType: file.type }
  });
},

// Subsequent turns: text only
_sendTextMessage: async function(text) {
  await this._callA2A({ message: text });
},

// Core A2A call — creates or continues a context
_callA2A: async function(payload) {
  var oModel = this.getView().getModel("chat");
  oModel.setProperty("/isLoading", true);

  var url = this._contextId
    ? A2A_BASE + "/contexts/" + this._contextId + "/messages"
    : A2A_BASE + "/messages";

  var resp = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload)
  });
  var body = await resp.json();
  this._contextId = body.contextId;

  if (body.status === "input-required") {
    // HITL: save taskId, show approval card
    this._taskId = body.taskId;
    this._appendMessage("agent", body.message, true /* isHITL */);
  } else {
    this._appendMessage("agent", body.message, false);
    if (body.message?.includes("SUBMITTED"))
      oModel.setProperty("/phase", "SUBMITTED");
  }
  oModel.setProperty("/isLoading", false);
},

// HITL resume: called when user clicks Confirm in the approval card
onConfirmSubmit: async function() {
  var resp = await fetch(A2A_BASE + "/tasks/" + this._taskId + "/resume", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ approved: true })
  });
  var body = await resp.json();
  this._taskId = null;
  this._appendMessage("agent", body.message, false);
},

11. SAP Build Work Zone

The MTA publishes the agent UI app (agentui.zip) to the HTML5 Application Repository automatically. Integration steps:

  1. Role Collections — create DocAI_AppUser (AppUser) and DocAI_AppAdmin (AppAdmin + AppUser) in BTP Cockpit.
  2. Content Channel — Work Zone → Provider Manager → + New → HTML5 Apps → Fetch Content.
  3. Launchpad site — add the agent UI tile, assign to role collections, publish.
  4. Joule registration — AI Launchpad → Agent Builder → Add external agent → paste https://<srv>/a2a/WorkflowAgentService/.well-known/agent-card.json.

12. Key Decisions and Lessons Learned

  • @AGent.hitl is cleaner than the confirmed-flag pattern. The annotation keeps the handler code simple (one branch, not two), the task state machine handles the pause/resume, and the frontend has a single clear signal (status === 'input-required') to render the approval card.
  • One skill file per workflow phase, not one monolithic file. The framework concatenates all skill files. Overlapping or contradictory rules from different phases in a single file caused the LLM to skip pre-conditions. Splitting by phase solved this immediately.
  • Raise maxIncomingMessageLength before anything else. The default quota silently truncates payloads. A base64 PDF can easily exceed 1 MB. Set it to 5 MB+ before testing with real documents.
  • cds.connect.to() with cds.User.Privileged() is the right delegation pattern. The agent's XSUAA gate is the security boundary. Inner service calls with Privileged user avoid double-auth and keep inner services testable independently.
  • Native PDF vision eliminates an entire pipeline stage. Passing the raw PDF as a document content block to Claude removed the need for OCR pre-processing, text extraction libraries, and the associated error surface. Confidence scores from native vision were higher than from extracted text in all test cases.
  • Context ID gives the agent memory across turns. The A2A context persists the full conversation history on the server side. The frontend only needs to store and resend the context ID — no client-side history management needed.
  • Template fingerprint matching keeps extraction accuracy high across form types. A generic prompt handles most forms but a layout-specific prompt significantly improves confidence on complex forms. Auto-creating a DRAFT template on first upload and asking the user to confirm before activation gives a good balance between automation and control.

The @cap-js/agents framework keeps the surface area small: one CDS annotation, one TypeScript class, a handful of Markdown files. The complexity lives where it belongs — in your business logic, your prompt engineering, and your skill instructions — not in routing or protocol code.

entry.title: Re: Concur User Permission - Roles vs. Personas
entry.content: Hi, Persona-based access is a good direction. Grouping roles into personas and assigning the persona makes access easier to grant and to explain. On the Concur side: as far as I know, permission roles are assigned per user. Bundling them into personas is usually handled where access is provisioned, for example in your identity provider or HR-driven user provisioning, which then sets the Concur roles for each persona. Your SAP Concur support contact can confirm what your edition supports. One thing worth planning at the same time is how you will review access afterwards. Persona or role-based reviews ask a manager “should Anna keep the AP Clerk persona?”, and most managers approve, because the name tells them little. A risk-based review works better: the reviewer approves or rejects what the user can actually do, for example “can create a vendor and also approve payments to that vendor”, or “can submit and approve the same expense report”. Personas make granting access simpler. A risk review shows whether a persona combines duties that should be split. Disclosure: I work for smartGRC. Our Review module runs this kind of risk-based review, and Concur users and roles can be loaded through our data adapter. Happy to share an example if useful.

entry.title: Populating Purchase Requisition Descriptions from Maintenance Orders in SAP S/4HANA Cloud
entry.content:
The Business Problem 

When Purchase Requisitions are created from Maintenance Orders — whether for non-stock materials or lean services — the PR header description field remains empty by default. This creates a visibility problem for procurement teams. 

Current State (As-Is) 

PR header description is blank 

Item descriptions are populated from order components 

In app F2229 (Manage Purchase Requisitions – Professional), users see unnamed PRs 

Only the PR ID is visible — users must drill into each PR to understand its purpose 

Why This Happens 

Currently for Purchase Requisition the description field is nullable when PRs are created via APIs (internal or external). This design provides flexibility but requires the calling application to explicitly populate the description field if needed. 

Understanding the Solution

SAP provides the BAdI EAM_ORDER_EXT_MODIFY_PR specifically to allow customers to enhance Purchase Requisition data during creation from Maintenance Orders. 

Extension Point 

BAdI        : EAM_ORDER_MODIFY_PR_DATA

Interface: IF_EAM_ORDER_EXT_MODIFY_PR

Method  : MODIFY_PR_DATA

The BAdI includes an exporting parameter structure: 

PURCHASEREQUISITIONITEM TYPE EAM_ORDER_PR_DATA_EXT 

This structure was extended by SAP to include one additional field: 

PURREQNDESCRIPTION TYPE c LENGTH 40  " PR Header Description 

What You Can Do 

In your BAdI implementation, you have access to comprehensive data from the Maintenance Order: 

Available Data: 

Order Header: Description, Order ID, Order Type, Created By User, Priority, etc. 

Operation Details: Operation Description, Operation Number, Functional Location, Equipment 

Component Information: Material, Quantity, Requirement Date, Product Type (Material vs. Lean Service) 

You can construct a meaningful description string using any combination of these fields and populate the PURREQNDESCRIPTION field. The description is then automatically written to the PR header. 

Implement the BAdI

Note: The code shown in this section is an example implementation. Adapt the description formatting logic to match your organization's requirements and naming conventions. 

Step 1: Create BAdI Implementation 

Navigate to the Custom Logic app (or ABAP Development Tools in Eclipse) and create a new BAdI implementation: 

  • BAdI : EAM_ORDER_MODIFY_PR_DATA
  • Implementation Class: `CL_EX_EAM_ORDER_MODIFY_PR` (system-generated, use Z prefix as per your naming convention) 
  • Interface: `IF_EAM_ORDER_EXT_MODIFY_PR` 
  • Method: `MODIFY_PR_DATA` 
  • Description: "Populate PR Description from Maintenance Order" 

Step 2: BAdI Method Structure 

The BAdI interface IF_EAM_ORDER_EXT_MODIFY_PR contains the method MODIFY_PR_DATA with the following parameters: 

Importing Parameters: 

  • `MAINTORDER` (type `I_MaintenanceOrderTP`) — Maintenance Order header data 
  • `MAINTORDEROPERATION` (type `I_MaintenanceOrderOperationTP`) — Operation-level data 
  • `MAINTORDEROPCOMPONENT_2` (type `I_MaintOrderOpComponentTP_2`) — Component data (current version) 
  • `MAINTORDEROPCOMPONENT` (type `I_MaintOrderOpComponentTP`) — Component data (deprecated, kept for compatibility) 

Exporting Parameter: 

  • `PURCHASEREQUISITIONITEM` (type `EAM_ORDER_PR_DATA_EXT`) — The structure where you populate PR fields, including the new field `PURREQNDESCRIPTION` 

The key field added to the exporting structure is: 

PURREQNDESCRIPTION TYPE c LENGTH 40  " PR Header Description 

Step 3: Sample Implementation 

The following code demonstrates three different approaches to populate the PR description. SAP provides these as commented examples in the generated implementation class. 

Implementation Option 1 — Use Maintenance Order Description 

This is the simplest approach: directly map the Maintenance Order header description to the PR. 

METHOD if_eam_order_ext_modify_pr~modify_pr_data. 
 
  " Option 1: Map the Maintenance Order Description directly 
  purchaserequisitionitem-purreqndescription = maintorder-maintenanceorderdesc. 
 
ENDMETHOD. 

Implementation Option 2 — Use Operation Description 

If your organization works at the operation level and operation descriptions are more meaningful: 

METHOD if_eam_order_ext_modify_pr~modify_pr_data. 
 
  " Option 2: Map the Maintenance Operation Description 
  purchaserequisitionitem-purreqndescription = maintorderoperation-operationdescription. 
 
ENDMETHOD. 

Implementation Option 3 — Build Custom Description 

For more context, combine multiple fields such as Order creator and Order description: 

METHOD if_eam_order_ext_modify_pr~modify_pr_data. 
 
  " Option 3: Build custom description with creator and order description 
  purchaserequisitionitem-purreqndescription = |{ maintorder-createdbyuser } { maintorder-maintenanceorderdesc }|. 
 
ENDMETHOD. 

Step 4: Activate 

Save and activate your BAdI implementation. The logic will execute automatically whenever a Purchase Requisition is created from a Maintenance Order. 

Important Behavior Note: BAdI Execution on PR Modification 

The EAM_ORDER_EXT_MODIFY_PR BAdI is triggered not only when a Purchase Requisition is created from a Maintenance Order, but also when an existing Purchase Requisition is modified from the Maintenance Order.

entry.title: HCM Job Architecture Harmonization in M&A Projects
entry.content:
HCM Job Architecture Harmonization in M&A Projects

1. Purpose and when to harmonize

An acquired workforce arrives with its own jobs, levels, titles, and pay structures. A lift-and-shift carries those over as they are by creating placeholders. Harmonization maps them into the acquirer’s job architecture so both populations run on a single, consistent structure in the target system. This guide covers how harmonization is carried out, the practices that work, how clients typically approach it, and the issues they run into.

Dimension

Lift-and-shift

Harmonize

What happens to acquired jobs

Loaded as separate job codes, levels, and grades

Mapped to the acquirer’s (or a combined) job codes, levels, and grades

Speed to Day 1

Faster; few decisions needed

Slower; needs design, compensation, and legal decisions and approvals

Effort later

Higher: two structures to maintain, split reporting

Lower: one structure, one governance process

Employee impact

Little visible change

Possible title, level, or grade changes; needs careful communication

Best fit

Short transition period, or the acquired entity stays separate

Workforce will be integrated long-term with shared reporting, pay cycles, and mobility

 

How to decide whether harmonization is the right call?

  • The acquired employees will sit in the same organization, reporting lines, and manager population as existing employees.
  • Compensation planning, promotion cycles, and performance processes will be shared.
  • Leadership expects combined workforce reporting by job family, level, or grade.
  • The acquirer wants one career framework and wants to avoid maintaining two architectures.
  • Timeline of HCM TSA Exit

 

2. Anatomy of a job architecture

A job architecture is the structure that organizes every role in the company. Harmonization means aligning each of these components, not just job codes.

Component

What it defines

SF EC representation

Job family and function

Broad groupings of work (Finance, Engineering, HR, Operations)

Job Function; job family via Job Profile Builder or a custom object

Job profile / job code

The standard definition of a role

Job Classification (job code) foundation object

Level

Scope and seniority within a family

Job Level (picklist or foundation object)

Grade and pay structure

Pay ranges, bands, or steps tied to level

Pay Grade, Pay Range, Pay Components

Titles

Job title (system) vs. business title (what people see)

Job title on job information; business title as a separate field

Classification attributes

Exempt/non-exempt, EEO category, regulatory or country-specific classification

Attributes on Job Classification; country-specific fields

Career paths

How people move across levels and families

Job Profile Builder or career content, or documented outside the system

Position structure (if used)

Seats in the org tied to a job code

Position Management objects

3. High Level Source to target mapping

Common source concept

Typical SF EC target

Job Family Group

Job Function or grouping in Job Profile Builder

Job Family

Job family / sub-function (Job Profile Builder or custom object)

Job Profile

Job Classification (job code)

Management Level

Job Level

Compensation Grade / Grade Profile

Pay Grade and Pay Range

Worker type / time type

Employee Class, Employment Type, Regular/Temporary

Position or job management staffing model

Position Management on or off

Worker-level business title

Business title field

Profile attributes (exempt status, EEO)

Job Classification attributes

 

4. Key design decisions

These decisions shape the step-by-step approach that follows. Agree them early, ideally before detailed mapping begins.

Decision

Options

Guidance

Level alignment

Adopt the acquirer’s levels, or map by scope

Match on scope of impact and accountability; calibrate on a sample of roles with business leaders

Titles

Keep legacy titles for a period, or convert at go-live

Separate the system job title from the business title to reduce friction for employees

Pay mapping

Map by grade equivalence, or by pay range overlap

Use range overlap; set a policy for out-of-range incumbents (hold, freeze, review at next cycle)

Exempt / non-exempt status

Keep source classification, or reassess

Treat any reclassification as a legal decision with overtime and payroll implications

Country rules

Single global mapping, or country exceptions

Plan exceptions where local law, collective agreements, or works council rights apply (for example Germany, France, and the Netherlands)

Number of job codes

Consolidate aggressively, or preserve granularity

Consolidate duplicates, but avoid losing granularity needed for market pricing and compliance

Staffing model

Position management or job management

Decide early; it affects headcount control, approvals, and reporting

Effective date

At go-live, or after the transition period or next pay cycle

Choose based on legal review, pay cycle timing, and what employees can absorb

History

Keep legacy codes in history, or remap

Keep a legacy-to-target reference so reporting can bridge both

 

5. How harmonization is done: step by step

Common issues clients face, and how to handle them, are noted under each step.

Step 1: Discover and inventory

  • Extract all jobs from the source: job code, title, family, level, grade, exempt status, country, and headcount by job.
  • Collect the acquirer’s architecture: job catalog, leveling guide, pay structures, title conventions, and any market pricing data.
  • Identify countries with local requirements, such as works council involvement or collective agreements.

Common issues and how to handle them

  • Messy job inventory. Duplicate, inactive, and single-person job codes build up over years. Clean and consolidate them here, and agree rules for legacy and single-incumbent codes before mapping.

Step 2: Set design principles and the target model

  • Choose the target: the acquirer’s architecture, a hybrid with extensions for specialist roles, or a new combined model.
  • Agree with the principles, for example: no pay reductions, no automatic title demotions, minimize new job codes, country compliance first.
  • Decide title policy, the level-matching method, and who owns the architecture after go-live.
  • Get executive approval of the principles before detailed mapping begins.

Common issues and how to handle them

  • Unclear ownership. There is often no single owner of job architecture on the acquirer side. Name an owner and an approver at kickoff, and start a decision log.
  • Staffing model mismatch. Source and target may handle positions and headcount differently. Decide the model early, and confirm during testing that approvals and headcount reporting behave as intended.
  • Timeline pressure. Harmonization decisions often take longer than the build and test windows. Prioritize high-headcount jobs, and use an interim crosswalk with phased employee-facing changes if needed.

Step 3: Build the crosswalk

The crosswalk is the core deliverable: a line by line mapping from every source job to a target job. Match on scope, accountability, required skills, and typical pay range, not on titles alone.

Crosswalk field

Purpose

Source job code, title, family, level, grade

Identify the starting point

Headcount and countries

Prioritizes review and shows where local rules apply

Target job code, title, family, level, grade

The proposed destination

Match type

One to one, many to one, one to many, no match, or exception

Confidence (high / medium / low)

Focus review time on uncertain matches

Pay impact

Flags incumbents outside the target range

Legal or works council flag

Marks items needing consultation or counsel review

Approver and status

Creates accountability and an audit trail

 

Match type

Description

Typical treatment

One-to-one

Source job equals a target job

Map directly

Many-to-one

Several source jobs collapse into one target job

Consolidate - check that pay and scope differences are acceptable

One-to-many

One source job split by scope or level

Split by criteria such as level, team, or country

No match

No equivalent in the target

Create a new job code under governance, or map to the closest with approval

Exception

Any country specific or regulated roles

Keep a separate mapping; involve legal and local HR

Common issues and how to handle them

  • Level mismatch. The same title can mean different scope in each company. Match on scope, accountability, and typical pay, and calibrate with business leaders on a sample of roles.

Step 4: Validate and approve

  • Review with HR Center of Excellence, Compensation, Legal, local HR, and business leaders. Start with the jobs covering most of the employees.
  • Run impact analysis for acquired company employees: how many people see a change in title, level, grade, exempt status, or pay position.
  • Engage works councils or employee representatives (unions etc.) where required and build their timeline into the plan.
  • Record every approval in a decision log and set a freeze date after which changes follow change control.

Common issues and how to handle them

  • Pay misalignment. Acquired pay can sit outside the target range for the mapped grade. Run the incumbent impact analysis, set an out-of-range policy, and get Compensation approval.
  • Legal and works council constraints. Job grouping and classification can be subject to co-determination or collective agreements. Identify the countries early, involve legal and local HR, and allow consultation time in the plan.
  • Exempt status changes. Classification practices differ between companies. Require counsel sign-off, and model overtime and payroll impact before any change.
  • Late changes after the freeze. Leaders often challenge matches once mock loads begin. Enforce the freeze date, impact assessment, and change control, and quantify the rework.

Step 5: Configure in SuccessFactors

  • Create or update job classifications, functions, levels, pay grades and ranges, and picklists with correct effective dates.
  • Set country-specific attributes, and position structures if position management is in use.
  • Align related configuration that depends on job data: role-based permissions, workflows, compensation and performance templates, and recruiting templates.

Common issues and how to handle them

  • Missed downstream dependencies. Payroll, recruiting, benefits, workflows, and reports are often keyed to job code, level, or grade. List every dependency during design, configure each one, and test it with real data in Step 6.

Step 6: Migrate and test

  • Apply the crosswalk in the data load: each employee’s job information is populated from the mapped target values.
  • Run mock loads with reconciliation by job code, level, grade, and country, and list any incumbent with no match.
  • Test downstream systems that depend on job data: payroll, applicant tracking, benefits eligibility, approval workflows, and reporting.

Common issues and how to handle them

  • History and effective dating. Past job records reference legacy codes. Decide whether history keeps the legacy codes or is remapped, and keep a legacy-to-target reference table for reporting.

Step 7: Communicate and govern

  • Brief managers and HR business partners first, with FAQs and talking points. Then communicate to employees.
  • Set up a job-code request process, naming standards, and a periodic review so the architecture does not sprawl after go-live.
  • Retire or lock legacy codes once reporting and history requirements are met.

Common issues and how to handle them

  • Perceived demotions or promotions. Title or level changes are visible to employees and managers. Apply the no-decrease and title principles set in Step 2, keep business titles separate from system titles, and brief managers first.

entry.title: Set up LeanIX' custom discovery connector just by talking to it
entry.content:
Last time, I showed you how to pull data from any API endpoint into SAP LeanIX with the custom discovery connector - and I promised a follow-up where we'd do the whole thing conversationally, without clicking through the product at all.. Things one does when being in Forth Worth, Texas, on Halloween and right before ASUG Tech Connect 2026. 

The trick is the SAP LeanIX MCP server. It exposes LeanIX as a set of tools an AI agent can call over the Model Context Protocol, so instead of building a connector in the UI, I just describe what I want to my AI buddy and let it drive. I set one connection up live - syncing my own Microsoft 365 calendar into LeanIX - and I'll walk you through exactly how it went. Mapping calendar events onto Objective fact sheets is a deliberately throwaway demo.  Swap in whatever source and fact-sheet type actually matter to you; the mechanics are the point, but everyone has that Microsoft Graph API at hand for trying this out.

The conversation

Once the MCP server was connected, I asked my AI client to show me what was already there:

"List all Custom Discovery Connector integrations."

It came back with the handful already in my workspace. So far so good. Let's make a new one:

"Set up a new custom discovery connector. Call it 'Weekly Calendar', pull this week's events from my Microsoft 365 calendar via the Graph calendarView endpoint, and map them to Objective fact sheets. Manual sync for now."

Behind the scenes the agent picked up the LeanIX setup skill, confirmed the details back to me in a little plan table, and - once I said "go ahead" - created the connector.

It writes the code, you review it

Next the agent pulled the connector's code instructions and asked how I wanted to authenticate (it offered OAuth2 client credentials, a Bearer token, or delegated OAuth). It then wrote the fetch script itself - a compact JavaScript that calls the Graph, pages through the results, and returns items in the shape the connector expects.

I didn't type a line of that. The agent validated it, then test-ran it against the live API (50 events came back with a next-page cursor) and only then pasted it, declaring graph.microsoft.com on the connector's allowed-hosts list so the sandbox will let it out.

It proposes the mapping

With a data sample in hand, the agent switched to the mapping skill and proposed how each event field should land on an Objective:

Source fieldObjective field
subjectName
idExternal ID (the match / dedup key)
bodyPreviewDescription
start.dateTimeLifecycle → active
end.dateTimeLifecycle → done

Choosing External ID as the match key is the important bit. It decides whether the next run updates an existing Objective or creates a new one, so point it at a stable identifier from your source. I eyeballed the proposal, said "save it," and the agent ran a preview (a dry run) before persisting the mapping. 

Sync, then review before anything is real

Finally:

"Trigger a sync and show me what came back."

The agent fired the sync, pulled the analytics, and reported back: 62 calendar events, all queued as create, zero conflicts, zero errors. With a sample of the first few and a question: commit all 62, or pick a subset? Nothing touches the inventory until you confirm, exactly like the review area in the UI.

And that was it. Listing, creating, coding, testing, mapping, syncing - one chat, a couple of minutes, no wizard.

Wrap up

Now I summarized two ways of setting up custom integrations via custom discovery connector: Use the UI or go fully agentic. For now, that's it, but I want to try out one more idea and then blog about it: What if your source isn't reachable via API, but you still want to push data into LeanIX? We shall see about that. 

For now: Happy Halloween and see you at ASUG Tech Connect 2026!?

entry.title: SAP TechEd 2026 — Day 3: O Grand Finale
entry.content:
SAP TechEd 2026 — Day 3: O Grand Finale


E aí, pessoal! Terceiro e último dia de SAP TechEd 2026. Confesso que bateu aquela mistura de "quero mais" com "preciso digerir tudo isso". Acompanhei o evento virtual daqui de Curitiba e, pra quem ficou até o final, o Day 3 trouxe aquele conteúdo que nem sempre vira manchete mas que, na prática, é o que mais muda o dia a dia de quem trabalha com SAP.

Se você caiu de paraquedas aqui, dá uma passada nos posts anteriores. No Day 1 falei do Enterprise AI Gateway, do modelo de IA rodando na Estação Espacial e das novidades pra quem é de ABAP. No Day 2 teve o Kasimir (aquele gato espião que roubou a cena), os 300 agentes prontos, robôs autônomos na fábrica da Intel e a festa dos 30 anos. Agora vamos pro gran finale.

Sem dados bons, não tem IA que salve

Todo mundo fala de agente, de IA generativa, de automação. Mas o Day 3 deixou claro uma coisa: nada disso funciona se os dados da empresa forem uma bagunça. E a SAP parece ter entendido isso.

O SAP Business Data Cloud ganhou um tal de Ontology Manager — basicamente uma ferramenta pra definir como os dados se relacionam entre si, mesmo quando vem de fontes diferentes (SAP e não-SAP). Parece abstrato? Pense assim: é o que permite você perguntar "qual cliente mais comprou no último trimestre?" pro Joule e ele realmente entender a pergunta, porque sabe qual tabela é cliente, qual é pedido e como elas se conectam.

Algo que me chamou atenção: a SAP fechou parceria com a Dremio pra montar um lakehouse dentro do BDC, com suporte a Apache Iceberg e Apache Polaris. Pra quem não é da área de dados, isso significa que dá pra consultar dados de vários repositórios sem copiar nada — o dado fica onde está, você só consulta.

Tem também a expansão do SAP Databricks e a integração com o SAP Reltio (aquela empresa que a SAP comprou em maio) pra master data. Ou seja: a SAP tá montando uma camada de dados que não fica só no mundo SAP. Isso muda o jogo.

O dev ganhou brinquedos novos

Se você é desenvolvedor, esse dia foi pra você.

Primeiro: dá pra construir agentes usando CrewAI e LangGraph direto na BTP. São frameworks open source que a galera já conhece do mundo Python, agora com identidade, autorização e governança da SAP por baixo. Isso é grande. Significa que você não precisa aprender um framework proprietário pra começar — pode usar o que já sabe.

Segundo: a integração com n8n dentro do Joule Studio. Pra quem não conhece, n8n é uma ferramenta de automação de workflows (tipo um Zapier open source). Agora dá pra desenhar workflows visuais e rodar dentro do ambiente SAP. Clientes early adopter já estão testando.

E tem os MCP Servers locais pra CAP, Fiori elements, SAPUI5 e mobile dev kit. Na prática, isso permite que assistentes de código como Cursor, Claude Code, Cline e Windsurf entendam o contexto SAP do seu projeto. Você abre o VS Code, pede pro assistente gerar um serviço CAP e ele já sabe o que é uma entity, uma annotation, um draft.

E o HANA Cloud agora também tem suporte a MCP — agentes podem consultar dados relacionais, espaciais e até fazer busca semântica com vetores. O detalhe legal: o HANA pode servir de memória de longo prazo pros agentes, mantendo contexto entre sessões.

O que vem por aí

Algumas coisas anunciadas ainda não estão disponíveis, então anota aí no calendário:

Até o final de 2026: Joule ganha funcionalidades de administração de banco no HANA Cloud, um modelo de decisão pra tarefas como aprovação de pedidos, e o Sovereign Cloud passa a rodar SAP AI Core e Datasphere no Reino Unido, Austrália e Canadá.

Pro primeiro trimestre de 2027: chega o SAP Enterprise AI Gateway (aquele que centraliza toda a governança de IA), as novas capacidades do Knowledge Graph com dados do cliente, a versão final do SAP-RPT-2.0 com detecção de anomalias, e o lakehouse com Dremio.

E até dezembro desse ano, rodar agentes customizados no runtime do Joule Studio continua gratuito pra clientes selecionados. A certificação de Joule Studio Developer também é free até 31 de dezembro. Se você tá pensando em começar, esse é o momento.

Fechando a mala (virtual)

Três dias de evento é muita coisa. Vou ser honesto: não dá pra absorver tudo em tempo real. Mas o que ficou pra mim foi isso: a SAP não tá mais só falando de IA. Ela tá entregando ferramentas, runtime, governança e uma camada de dados que conecta o mundo SAP com o resto. E abriu o jogo pra frameworks que a comunidade já usa.

Pra quem é de ABAP como eu, o recado é claro: o ABAP não vai morrer, mas vai mudar. MCP Server, VS Code, modelos de IA treinados em código ABAP — quem se adaptar vai surfar essa onda. Quem ficar parado... bom, você já sabe.

Todo o conteúdo está disponível on demand no SAP TechEd Virtual — é gratuito e vale cada minuto.

Quer ver o recap do Day 3? Assista o SAP Developer News — TechEd Berlin Day 3.

Se esses posts te ajudaram de alguma forma, deixa um Kudo lá na SAP Community — ajuda demais a comunidade de Curitiba a continuar trazendo conteúdo em português. E se tiver dúvida ou quiser trocar ideia, comenta aqui.

entry.title: SAP BTP Cockpit now introduces Scripting and Automation Preview panel
entry.content:
Automate Everything: A Deep Dive into SAP BTP's Scripting & Automation Preview

Introduction

If you have ever set up an SAP BTP subaccount manually — clicking through the cockpit, filling in forms, waiting for confirmations — you know how repetitive and error-prone that process can be, especially at scale. SAP BTP has quietly introduced a game-changing feature right inside the BTP Cockpit: Scripting & Automation Preview.

This feature bridges the gap between point-and-click administration and true infrastructure-as-code, giving developers and platform engineers an instant script for every action they take in the cockpit — in SAP BTP CLI, Cloud Foundry CLI, and Terraform flavors.

What Is Scripting & Automation Preview?

Scripting & Automation Preview is a contextual code panel built directly into the SAP BTP Cockpit. For every page you are on — subaccount overview, entitlements, Cloud Foundry environments, service instances — the panel displays the equivalent SAP BTP CLI, Cloud Foundry CLI, and Terraform commands automatically. Crucially, it updates in real time as you navigate: no refresh, no manual lookup, no copy-pasting values from the UI into a docs page.

The panel is accessible via the <> icon in the top-right corner of the BTP Cockpit toolbar (see the screenshot below — it is highlighted in the navigation bar). Once activated, it docks at the bottom of the screen. As you move from one cockpit page to another, the panel silently updates its content to match your current context, making the transition from UI-based actions to scripted or infrastructure-as-code workflows completely frictionless — with no manual research required.

The Scripting & Automation Preview panel in the SAP BTP Cockpit, showing CLI commands auto-generated for a Global & subaccount 

The Six Tabs — What Each One Gives You

The panel is organized into six tabs across three scripting paradigms, each serving a specific use case in the DevOps and platform engineering workflow:

SAP BTP CLI

1. CLI

The CLI tab generates ready-to-run SAP BTP CLI (btp) commands for the resource currently in view. This is the primary CLI for managing BTP platform resources — global accounts, subaccounts, entitlements, and environments.

For the "Mars" subaccount shown in the screenshot, it generates three commands automatically:

# Get the current subaccount
btp get accounts/subaccount "10a...8a2f15"

# Create the subaccount
btp create accounts/subaccount \
  --display-name "Mars" \
  --region "eu11" \
  --subdomain "mars" \
  --beta-enabled "true"

# Update the subaccount
btp update accounts/subaccount "1...15" \
  --display-name "Mars" \
  --beta-enabled "true"

Each command block has a "View Documentation" link alongside it — so you can jump straight to the official BTP CLI reference for that specific command. No more hunting through docs to find the right flag.

2. CLI Setup

The CLI Setup tab provides the prerequisite setup commands needed before the BTP CLI commands will work — things like installing the BTP CLI, logging in to your global account, and targeting the right subaccount. This is invaluable for onboarding new team members or setting up CI/CD pipelines from scratch.

Cloud Foundry CLI

3. CF CLI

The CF CLI tab generates Cloud Foundry CLI (cf) commands for the current cockpit page. Where the BTP CLI covers platform-level resources (subaccounts, entitlements, service subscriptions), the CF CLI covers runtime-level resources: orgs, spaces, apps, services, buildpacks, routes, and environment variables.

For a Cloud Foundry environment page, the panel might surface commands like:

# Target the Cloud Foundry org and space
cf login -a "https://api.cf.eu11.hana.ondemand.com"
cf target -o "my-org" -s "dev"

# Create a Cloud Foundry space
cf create-space "dev" -o "my-org"

This is particularly valuable because the cf command surface is vast, and remembering the exact syntax for service binding, role assignment, or environment variable management is non-trivial. The panel handles that for you.

4. CF CLI Setup

The CF CLI Setup tab provides the commands needed to install and authenticate the Cloud Foundry CLI — including the API endpoint specific to your BTP region — so a new pipeline or developer machine can be configured with a single copy-paste.

Terraform

5. Terraform

The Terraform tab generates a Terraform HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) configuration block equivalent to the current cockpit state. This is the bridge between the visual cockpit and infrastructure-as-code:

resource "btp_subaccount" "mars" {
  display_name = "Mars"
  subdomain    = "mars"
  region       = "eu11"
  beta_enabled = true
}

With this output, you can bootstrap your Terraform codebase directly from the cockpit without having to manually author resource blocks from scratch.

6. Terraform Setup

The Terraform Setup tab gives you the provider configuration and backend setup code needed to get Terraform running with the SAP BTP Terraform Provider. It includes the required_providers block and authentication setup — removing all the boilerplate research.

A note on tabs visible in the screenshot: The screenshot shows four tabs — CLI, CLI Setup, Terraform, and Terraform Setup. The Cloud Foundry CLI tabs appear contextually when you navigate to a Cloud Foundry environment page within your subaccount. The full panel adapts its available tabs based on what resource type is currently in view.

Why This Feature Matters

For Platform Engineers: Shift Left on Automation

Historically, BTP Admins or teams would set up BTP resources manually in the cockpit during a project's early phases and only later "clean up" by writing CLI scripts or Terraform configs. The Scripting & Automation Preview collapses that timeline. You can write automation from day one — with zero risk of the script diverging from what was actually provisioned, because the cockpit generates it from the live resource state.

For Developers: No More CLI Reference Hunting

The BTP CLI is powerful but has hundreds of commands and flags. Remembering the exact syntax for btp create accounts/subaccount — including all the required and optional parameters — is a cognitive burden. With this feature, the cockpit tells you the exact command to run, pre-filled with the real values of your current resource.

For DevOps Teams: Reproducible Environments

One of the hardest problems in BTP operations is reproducibility. "Works in dev, doesn't work in prod" often traces back to configuration drift. When you can generate the exact Terraform or CLI script from a known-good environment, you get a reliable blueprint for spinning up identical environments elsewhere.

For Auditors and Compliance Teams

Every command the panel generates corresponds to a real API call against the BTP accounts service. Combined with the Open in Audit Log Viewer link visible in the subaccount overview, you have a complete trail from human intention → machine command → audit log.

A Real-World Scenario: Bootstrapping a New Subaccount

Let me walk through exactly how this feature speeds up a real task.

Scenario: You need to create a new "Production" subaccount mirroring the "Mars" dev subaccount, in the same region, with the same settings.

Old way (15–20 minutes):

  1. Open BTP Cockpit.
  2. Navigate to the global account.
  3. Click "Create Subaccount", fill in the form.
  4. Separately, open BTP CLI docs and find btp create accounts/subaccount.
  5. Write the command manually, referring to the form values.
  6. Copy the command into your runbook or automation script.

New way with Scripting & Automation Preview (2–3 minutes):

  1. Open the "Mars" subaccount in BTP Cockpit.
  2. Click the <> icon to open the Scripting & Automation panel.
  3. Copy the Create Subaccount CLI command from the CLI tab.
  4. Adjust --display-name and --subdomain for production.
  5. Run or paste into your pipeline script.

The Terraform tab gives you an equivalent HCL block you can drop straight into your main.tf.

Beta Features: Why It's Enabled

Notice in the screenshot that Beta Features: Enabled is shown for the Mars subaccount. The Scripting & Automation Preview is currently in preview/beta status — you need beta features enabled at the subaccount level to access it. This is straightforward to enable via:

btp update accounts/subaccount <subaccount-id> --beta-enabled "true"

Ironically, the panel itself shows you this command once beta is enabled — self-referential and elegant.

Getting Started

Here's what you need to begin using Scripting & Automation Preview:

StepAction
1Log in to SAP BTP Cockpit
2Navigate to your target subaccount
3Enable Beta Features in subaccount settings
4Click the <> icon in the top-right toolbar
5Navigate your resources — the panel updates automatically
6Copy commands from CLI, Terraform, or their respective setup tabs

Current Scope and Limitations

As with any preview feature, there are things to be aware of:

  • Preview status means the generated scripts should be reviewed before being used in production pipelines — commands, flags, and Terraform resource schemas may evolve as the feature matures.
  • Coverage across resource types is expanding with each BTP Cockpit release. Some edge-case configurations may not yet have complete equivalents in all three scripting paradigms.
  • The panel's tabs adapt to context: BTP CLI tabs appear for subaccount/entitlement pages, CF CLI tabs appear for Cloud Foundry environment pages. Not all tab types are visible on every page — this is by design, not a gap.
  • Copy-paste is currently the primary integration mechanism. Direct export to a file or a Git repository would be a powerful next step.

What's Next?

The direction this feature points toward is clear: SAP wants every action in the BTP Cockpit to be scriptable by default. The logical next steps could include:

  • Session recording — capture a full sequence of cockpit actions as a single script or Terraform plan.
  • Export to file — download the generated scripts directly rather than copy-pasting.
  • CI/CD integration — push generated configs directly to a connected Git repository.
  • Drift detection — compare the live cockpit state against a stored Terraform state file and highlight differences.

Conclusion

Scripting & Automation Preview is one of those features that sounds simple but has significant implications for how teams manage BTP infrastructure. It removes friction from the shift to infrastructure-as-code, accelerates developer onboarding, and makes reproducibility a default rather than an afterthought.

The feature's core design principle is elegant: whatever page you are on, the cockpit tells you how to do it from the command line or in code — automatically, without you asking. SAP BTP CLI for platform resources. Cloud Foundry CLI for runtime resources. Terraform for everything you want to version-control and replay. The panel stays in sync as you navigate, so you never lose context.

If you are running SAP BTP with beta features enabled, open the <> panel the next time you configure a subaccount or set up a Cloud Foundry space. Within minutes, you will have ready-to-run CLI commands and Terraform blocks — generated from the live state of your environment, pre-filled with real values, and linked directly to the official documentation.

That is not just convenient. That is a fundamentally better way to operate cloud infrastructure.

Why Central Finance postings fail, and where SAP AIF fits in?

 

 

 

You replicate a document from a source system, and Central Finance refuses it. Maybe the period isn't open yet. Maybe a cost center got blocked last week. Maybe a master data mapping points at nothing.

Someone has to spot the failure, work out whose problem it is, and push the document through again. In Central Finance, that someone works in SAP Application Interface Framework, or AIF. Think of it as the inbox for every posting that didn't make it.

 

 

Failures don't vanish. They wait in AIF until the cause is fixed and the message is restarted or cancelled.

One gap to know about. AIF covers the Central Finance replication scenarios, but not the FI/CO initial load interface. If an initial load posting fails, you won't find it here.

Who fixes what. Most failures land in one of three buckets, and each has a different owner.

 

Agree this split before go-live. It saves days of tickets bouncing around.
