entry.title: Bulk Create and Update Mitigating Controls in SAP GRC Access Control
entry.content:
Introduction

Anyone who has worked on SAP GRC Access Control implementations will know the effort of creating and maintaining mitigating controls , especially when the same set must be loaded into several environments. The standard Mitigating Controls screen handles one control at a time. Each control needs an organisation, a business process and subprocess, an approver, monitors and the risks it mitigates. For a handful of controls this is fine. For a few hundred, it is slow and error prone.

For the manual steps, see this article on creating mitigation controls: https://community.sap.com/t5/financial-management-blog-posts-by-members/sap-grc-10-0-10-1-12-0-creation-of-mitigation-controls/ba-p/13257231

This post describes a custom ABAP report that creates or updates mitigating controls in bulk from an input file. It was built and tested on the following release:

Objective

Replicate the standard screen, but faster, without bypassing any standard GRC validations.

The report does not write to database tables directly. It calls the standard GRC classes and methods in the same sequence as the screen: open a session, lock the control, update, save, unlock. Standard authorisation checks, locking and change logs therefore behave exactly as they do for manual maintenance. The selection screen, file F4 help and logging follow the pattern of the standard report GRFN_MDUG.

Program Name

The below screenshot shows the custom program ZR_WCE_MASS_MITICTRLS_CREATION, which is used to initiate the bulk mitigating-control creation/update process. Running the program opens the upload screen where the template file can be selected and processed.

Users choose a tab delimited or CSV file, set the delimiter, and run in one of two modes:

  • Test run: validates every record and reports what would be created or updated. Nothing is written.
  • Create / update run: writes the controls after a confirmation that names the system and client.

A control ID that does not exist is created. One that already exists is updated.

The Download Template button saves a ready to fill file. It has nine columns:

  1. MIT_ID (control ID, up to 10 characters)
  2. TITLE (up to 40 characters)
  3. DESCRIPTION
  4. ORG_UNIT (organisation name or object ID)
  5. AC_BPROC (business process)
  6. AC_BSUBPROC (business subprocess)
  7. APPROVER
  8. MONITORS (separated by semicolons)
  9. RISK_IDS (separated by semicolons)

 

Selecting the file and running in Test run only mode allows users to specify the file format and delimiter and then run the process initially to identify any issues before committing the changes.

Validations

Every record is checked for column count, field lengths, mandatory fields and duplicate control IDs in the file. The organisation, business process and subprocess must exist, every risk must exist in the ruleset, and the approver and monitors must be valid SAP users. Inactive risks are skipped with a warning, and a record with no active risk left fails. All checks run for each record, so one pass shows everything wrong with it.

Organisation rule

Several organisation objects can carry the same name. The report uses the one whose Access Control owner list contains the approver and all monitors. If none does, the record fails with a message listing what was checked. Nothing is guessed.

Update behaviour

The file is the source of truth for the fields it carries: title, description, organisation, process, subprocess, approver, monitors and risks are replaced. Anything not in the file stays as it is. A control locked by another user fails with the standard lock message and is left untouched.

Results

Each record is saved on its own. A failed record is discarded and never affects the others. The result list shows one row per record with a status light, and a double click shows all its messages. Failures report the step that failed and the real GRC messages.

Where data is read and written

The report reads three tables directly with Open SQL:

  • USR02: confirms the approver and monitors are real users.
  • HRP1000: finds organisation objects by name or ID.
  • GRACSODRISK: confirms each risk exists and is active.

Everything else goes through standard classes:

  • Control data: CL_GRPC_API_CONTROL
  • Organisation owner list: CL_GRFN_API_EXT_AC_OWNER
  • Approver and monitors: CL_GRFN_API_EXT_AC_OWNER_CN
  • Risk link: CL_GRFN_API_EXT_AC_RISK (stored in HRT5320 by the API)
  • Process configuration: CL_GRAC_ERM_CONFIG

The persisted lock (GRFNLOCKOBJECT) is released through the standard unlock method.

Security

Front end file transfer is checked with S_GUI activity 61. Assign the report to an authorisation group (object S_PROGRAM) so only GRC administrators can run it. It uses no dynamic SQL, no native SQL and no server file access. File values are cleaned and length checked, text starting with =, + or @ is rejected to prevent spreadsheet formula injection, and run limits protect against oversized files.

Uploaded Mitigating Controls

The uploaded mitigating controls are shown in the Mitigating Controls work centre. The screen displays the control ID, title, and detailed control description, allowing users to review the controls created or updated through the bulk upload process.

Thank you for reading. I hope this program can help you in your GRC implementations to quickly create mitigating controls.

If you have questions, please drop a comment below.

You can also reach me directly at Maddysmail26@gmail.com whether it's a quick question, a deeper implementation challenge, or just a conversation about SAP.

Let's continue learning, sharing and building on each other's experience

entry.content:
Hello,

Thank you for your question!

Our internal AI chatbot has provided the following response. Please check whether it resolves the issue.

Kind regards,

Henrike

AI-Generated Content

Response to HR/Payroll Posting Governance on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition

Below is a structured analysis of both requirements, grounded in standard S/4HANA Public Cloud functionality and what the Knowledge Graph confirms about the relevant components.

Requirement 1 — HR Data Confidentiality & Dual-Level Reporting

The Core Challenge

In S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, the architecture is deliberately based on a Business Role + Restriction Type model (instead of direct authorization object field-level customization as in Private/On-Premise). This shapes what is achievable and how.

Recommended Architecture: Two-Tier Business Role Design

The correct approach combines Business Role scoping (IAM app) with Fiori tile visibility control and — where applicable — G/L account range restrictions.

Layer 1 — Fiori App Access (Role-Level Separation)

The two primary apps for journal entry visibility confirmed in the KG are:
  • Display Line Items in General Ledger — shows G/L line items with full account assignment detail (G/L account, Profit Center, Cost Center, Segment). This app explicitly supports filtering and grouping by these characteristics.
  • Manage Journal Entries — full Universal Journal line item access.
Action: Assign these apps only to the restricted Controlling/Regulatory role. General Finance users should receive only aggregated balance/report apps (e.g., balance sheet Fiori tiles) without drill-down to individual HR G/L line items.

Layer 2 — G/L Account Range Restriction via Restriction Types

In S/4HANA Public Cloud IAM, standard Business Roles carry Restriction Types for Financial Accounting. The most relevant:
 
Restriction Type Object Purpose
F_BKPF_BUK – Company CodeAccounting DocumentLimits access by company code
F_SKA1_BUK – G/L AccountChart of Accounts / G/L AccountRestricts which G/L account ranges are visible
K_CSKS – Cost CenterControlling Area / Cost CenterLimits which cost centers are accessible
K_PCA – Profit CenterControlling Area / Profit CenterLimits which profit centers are accessible
Practical configuration for your scenario:
  • General Finance role: Assign F_SKA1_BUK restriction excluding the HR G/L range (6100xxxxx). They access only the aggregated cost account group view. Do not assign the line-item drill-down apps to this role.
  • Controlling/Regulatory role: Full G/L range (including 61010000–61060000 range), full Cost Center and Profit Center access, with access to both line-item apps above.

Layer 3 — Important Limitations in Public Cloud

Critical constraint: SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition does not support custom ABAP code or true field-level data masking at the Universal Journal (ACDOCA) persistence layer. There is no native "data masking" product feature in the Public Cloud edition that would blank out specific field values while still allowing a user to open the document.
This means the dual-level visibility must be enforced entirely at the app/role access level, not at the data level. The Universal Journal retains all analytical detail regardless of role — what changes is which users can reach which apps and which account ranges.

Layer 4 — Reporting for the Restricted Group (Separazione Contabile)

For the Controlling/Regulatory team, the confirmed standard capability via the Display Line Items in General Ledger app supports:
  • Selection/filtering by G/L account, Cost Center, Profit Center
  • Export to Excel for regulatory submissions
  • Multi-company code reporting with display currency conversion
This is fully compatible with Separazione Contabile reporting requirements: users with the unrestricted role can select specifically the HR Profit Center hierarchy and HR G/L account range.

Requirement 2 — Profit Center Zero Balance & F24 Clearing

Root Cause

Your scenario is a classic document splitting imbalance: the HR payroll postings load specific Profit Centers (e.g., PC_DIRIG, PC_AGENT, etc.) but the F24 payment document is posted to a generic Profit Center ("GENER"). Without a Zero Balance compensating entry, the document splitting engine sees unresolved profit center segments.

Standard Solution: Zero Balance Indicator for Profit Center in Document Splitting

The SAP roadmap explicitly confirms this is an evolving capability. The KG contains a dedicated roadmap item:
Enabling mandatory document splitting per profit center
This confirms that mandatory document splitting per Profit Center is a tracked capability on the SAP roadmap for S/4HANA. In the current standard Public Cloud configuration, this is managed as follows:

How the Zero Balance Mechanism Works

When the Zero Balance indicator is set for the Profit Center characteristic in document splitting configuration, the system automatically generates compensating line items (using a defined Zero Balance Clearing Account, typically an intercompany or internal transit account) whenever a document would otherwise produce a non-zero profit center balance. This ensures:
  1. The original HR payables are posted to their specific Profit Centers.
  2. When the F24 payment clears against a generic Profit Center (GENER), the splitting rule fires and inserts compensating lines so that each Profit Center nets to zero within the document.
  3. The AP/tax authority vendor account is cleared completely.

Is Expert Configuration Required?

Yes, in S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, this requires Expert Configuration (also called "Self-Service Configuration" or Customizing via the "Manage Your Solution" / BAdI framework).
The relevant configuration path is:
Manage Your Solution → Configure Your Solution →
  Financial Accounting → General Ledger Accounting →
    Business Transactions → Document Splitting →
      Define Zero-Balance Clearing Account
      Define Document Splitting Characteristics for General Ledger Accounting
        → Profit Center → Set "Zero Balance" = Active
Important: In S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, the document splitting configuration is pre-activated (document splitting is always on and uses the standard splitting method). However, the Zero Balance indicator per characteristic is a configuration parameter that can be set independently for each characteristic (Profit Center, Segment, Business Area). It is not activated by default for Profit Center in all scenarios — it depends on the initial implementation configuration.

Recommended Configuration Steps

 
Step Action Where
1Verify that Profit Center is active as a splitting characteristicExpert Configuration / Configure Your Solution
2Set Zero Balance = Active for Profit Center characteristicDocument Splitting – Characteristics for G/L
3Define a dedicated Zero Balance Clearing G/L account (balance sheet, no open item management, both debit/credit postings allowed)Chart of Accounts + Expert Config
4Map F24 document type to the correct document splitting rule that includes the Zero Balance handlingDocument Splitting – Business Transaction Assignment
5Test: Post a sample payroll run followed by a simulated F24 paymentUnit test in quality system

Additional Consideration: Profit Center Derivation on the F24 Document

Even with Zero Balance activated, the F24 document must be able to derive the specific Profit Centers to split against. If the F24 is always posted to GENER, the zero-balance entries will compensate against GENER — which may still leave balances on the specific HR Profit Centers unless the derivation logic knows which HR Profit Centers to offset.
Two approaches:
  • Approach A (Preferred): Use Substitution Rules (BRF+ substitution in S/4HANA Cloud) to derive the correct Profit Center on the F24 tax line items at posting time, based on the G/L account range or cost center assignment of the underlying payroll posting.
  • Approach B: Accept the compensating zero-balance entries through GENER and perform a periodic reallocation (Universal Allocation) from GENER to the specific HR Profit Centers at period end.

Summary Table

 
Topic Mechanism Config Complexity
Dual-level FI visibilityBusiness Role + Restriction Types (G/L account range, Profit Center, Cost Center)Standard IAM config
Line-item detail for regulatory team"Display Line Items in General Ledger" app, restricted roleStandard app assignment
Data masking at field levelNot natively available in Public CloudN/A — enforce at app/role layer
Profit Center zero balance in doc splittingZero Balance indicator on Profit Center characteristicExpert Configuration required
F24 Profit Center derivationBRF+ Substitution RuleExpert Configuration
Periodic PC rebalancing (fallback)Universal AllocationStandard CO config
Disclaimer: The authorization object names (F_BKPF_BUK, K_CSKS, K_PCA, etc.) and the document splitting configuration path reflect standard SAP product documentation and general S/4HANA architecture knowledge. The specific behavior in your Public Cloud tenant — particularly which Expert Configuration activities are open to customer configuration vs. restricted by SAP — should be validated with your SAP Implementation Partner or via an SAP Expert Configuration engagement (SAP Service & Support).

Since you have the app now, maybe two things can save you some code and time. I read them today in a BTP ABAP Environment system (release 920). Data elements: BALOBJ_D, BALSUBOBJ, BALLOGHNDL and BALMNR are released there, BALNREXT and BALUSER are not. If your service is a custom entity, those two fields don't need a data element of your own, a built-in type with a label annotation should be enough (abap.char(100) for the external ID, abap.char(12) for the user). Performance: LOAD_LOGS_VIA_FILTER only takes FILTER and READ_ONLY_HEADER, there is no paging, so everything that matches the filter comes into memory before the query provider can page it. What I would try first is READ_ONLY_HEADER = abap_true for the list (the header already has counters like NUMBER_ERROR_ITEMS), LOAD_LOG with the handle only when the user opens one log, and passing the date filter of the list report to SET_TIME_INTERVAL, with SET_MAXIMUM_LOG_NUMBER as a cap. I also looked for a released CDS view on the log header, because with one you could select and page in SQL. R_ApplicationLogHeader is there, on BALHDR, but its contract is SAP_INTERNAL_API and it is not released, so your point stands. I didn't build or time any of this, so please tell me if it helps. #AI-Generated Content

Public Cloud Alternative for RFDOPR20

RFDOPR20 is a classic ABAP report for Accounts Receivable open items analysis (sorted by due date), part of the FI-GL-IS application component. In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, the transaction-code paradigm is replaced by SAP Fiori apps.

Recommended Fiori Alternative: Manage Customer Line Items (F0711)

The direct Public Cloud equivalent is the Fiori app F0711 — Manage Customer Line Items (S36 / Public Cloud 2602).

entry.title: Re: Leading zeros trimmed in Quantitative Master Inspecti...
entry.content:
Hi Vivek,

I don't think there is a setting for this, because the zero is gone before it reaches the database. In my S/4HANA 2020 lab the target value and the limits are floating point fields, type FLTP: QPMK-SOLLWERT, TOLERANZOB and TOLERANZUN, and the same fields in PLMK and QAMV. The results too, like QAMR-MITTELWERT and QASE-MESSWERT. A float only keeps the number, so 0120 and 120 are the same value there. To show it, QM calls QSS0_FLTP_TO_CHAR_CONVERSION, which passes just the value and the decimal places (QPMK-STELLEN) to FLTP_CHAR_CONVERSION, so I see no padding option on that path.

So the way I would look at it depends on what this value means for your client:

  • If it is a real measurement and the zeros are only a display format, keep the quantitative characteristic and format the value where people see it. In a form, certificate or report, for whole numbers, it can be something like |{ lv_int WIDTH = 4 PAD = '0' ALIGN = RIGHT }| after moving the float to an integer. For results recording, the enhancements QEEM0029 (characteristic overview) and QEEM0030 (single screen) give you a customer subscreen, where you could show the formatted value next to the standard one.
  • If it is really an identifier, like a grade or a class, then it isn't a number, and I would use a qualitative characteristic with codes. QPCD-CODE is CHAR 4, so 0120 stays 0120. The price is that you lose the numeric limits and the valuation against them.

If they only need to keep what was typed next to the result, QAMR-PRUEFBEMKT and QASE-PRUEFBEMKT are short text fields (CHAR 40).

What I measured: the field types in QPMK, PLMK, QAMV, QAMR and QASE, the code of QSS0_FLTP_TO_CHAR_CONVERSION, the QEEM enhancement list and interfaces, and QPCD-CODE. The ABAP line was only syntax checked. I didn't build the subscreen or test any of this in QS21 or QE51N, so try it in a sandbox first.

entry.title: SAP Joule Work at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026: Redefining the Future of Work with Agentic AI
entry.content:
How SAP is transforming enterprise productivity through an AI-native experience, intelligent agents, connected applications, and autonomous business execution.

The way we interact with enterprise software is about to change significantly.

For decades, employees have worked across multiple business applications, switching between screens, searching for information, navigating workflows, and coordinating activities across different departments. Even with automation and digital transformation, completing a business task often requires interaction with multiple systems.

But what if employees could simply describe what they want to accomplish, and AI could understand the objective, identify the required information, coordinate the relevant agents, and help complete the work?

This is the vision behind SAP Joule Work.

At SAP TechEd Berlin 2026, SAP announced significant advancements in Joule Work, demonstrating how enterprise AI is evolving beyond traditional conversational assistants toward intelligent, context-aware, and agent-driven business execution.

The announcement represents an important shift in SAP's user experience strategy: moving from application-centric interactions to an AI-native experience where business users can focus on outcomes rather than navigating individual applications.

Let's explore what is new in SAP Joule Work and why it matters for the future of enterprise productivity.

1. What Is SAP Joule Work?

 

SAP Joule Work is SAP's AI-powered work experience designed to bring business applications, AI assistants, and intelligent agents together through a unified interface.

Instead of interacting with every application independently, employees can use Joule Work as a central starting point for their daily business activities.

Users can express their requirements in natural language, interact with AI assistants, access relevant business information, and work with agents that help coordinate activities across connected enterprise systems.

The key idea is simple:

Don't make employees navigate the business. Let AI help employees get business work done.

SAP is positioning Joule Work as a new way of experiencing enterprise software, bringing intelligence and business execution closer to where employees actually work.

2. A Completely Redesigned AI-Native User Experience

 

One of the major announcements at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 is the redesigned Joule Work experience.

SAP has reimagined the user experience around a unified entry point, making it more intuitive to interact with business applications and AI capabilities.

The new experience brings together:

  • SAP business applications.

  • Microsoft 365.

  • Claude Cowork.

  • Glean.

  • ServiceNow.

  • SAP Joule Assistants and Joule Agents.

This is particularly interesting because enterprise employees rarely work within a single application ecosystem.

For example, a business user might need information from SAP S/4HANA, collaborate through Microsoft 365, retrieve organizational knowledge from Glean, and coordinate activities through ServiceNow.

Joule Work aims to bring these experiences together rather than forcing employees to continuously switch between different applications.

Another important capability is its ability to remember user preferences and context from previous interactions, allowing the experience to adapt to individual working patterns.

The business impact: A more consistent employee experience, reduced application switching, and easier access to business information and AI capabilities.

3. Conversations and Spaces: Two Important Ways of Working with Joule

 
SAP TechEd highlighted two important elements of the Joule Work experience: Conversations and Spaces.

Conversations – Interact with Enterprise AI Naturally

Conversations provide a natural-language interface for interacting with Joule.

Users can ask questions, request information, seek recommendations, and engage with assistants and agents to accomplish business tasks.

For example:

"Show me the latest sales performance, identify the regions that are below target, and summarize the key reasons for the decline."

Rather than manually navigating multiple reports, users can interact with Joule through a conversational experience to explore business information and obtain relevant insights.

The objective is to make enterprise intelligence accessible through natural interactions.

Spaces – Bring Business Information Together

Spaces provide a collaborative experience where information can be brought together into interactive, reusable work environments.

Instead of keeping business information scattered across conversations and applications, users can work with contextual information and interactive applications within a shared space.

For example, a sales team could use a dedicated space to bring together:

  • Sales performance information.

  • Customer account details.

  • Pipeline insights.

  • Business recommendations.

  • Relevant applications and workflows.

This creates a more structured way to collaborate around specific business objectives.

Why this matters: Conversations help employees interact with AI, while Spaces help organize information and work around business outcomes.

4. Agentic Thinking: Moving from Answering Questions to Completing Complex Workflows

 

This is arguably one of the most important advancements announced for Joule Work at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026.

Traditional AI assistants typically respond to individual prompts or perform predefined tasks.

However, enterprise business processes are rarely simple. A single business objective can involve multiple systems, data sources, departments, and decision points.

SAP is introducing new agentic thinking capabilities in Joule Work to help AI agents plan and orchestrate the steps required to complete complex, multistep business workflows.

These capabilities focus on:

  • Understanding the user's business objective.

  • Planning the steps required to achieve it.

  • Identifying relevant assistants and agents.

  • Coordinating activities across business domains.

  • Orchestrating execution across SAP and non-SAP systems.

A practical business example

Imagine a finance manager asking Joule Work:

"Analyze overdue customer invoices, identify high-risk accounts, prioritize collections activities, and prepare recommendations for the finance team."

This is not a simple question.

To support this request, the system needs to consider:

  1. Customer information and account details.

  2. Outstanding invoices and payment history.

  3. Payment terms and credit exposure.

  4. Relevant business rules.

  5. Prioritized collections recommendations.

With agentic thinking, Joule Work can plan and coordinate the activities required to address the request through relevant assistants and agents.

The goal is to move beyond individual AI responses toward coordinated business execution.

This is where enterprise AI becomes particularly powerful: AI is no longer just responding to instructions; it is helping orchestrate the work required to achieve business outcomes.

5. Open Agent Interoperability: Connecting SAP and Third-Party AI Agents

 

Enterprise AI will not operate within a single technology ecosystem.

Organizations are increasingly adopting different AI platforms, third-party agents, and specialized automation solutions.

Recognizing this, SAP is advancing Joule Work through open interoperability protocols, including:

  • Agent2Agent (A2A): Enables communication and collaboration between different AI agents.

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP): Enables AI applications and agents to connect with external tools and contextual information.

One important enhancement announced at TechEd is the ability for third-party agents to securely invoke Joule Agents through a governed agent gateway.

This creates opportunities for agents operating on different platforms to collaborate within enterprise workflows.

Example: Procurement workflow

Imagine an organization using a third-party procurement agent to identify potential supplier risks.

That agent could securely invoke relevant Joule Agents to obtain SAP business information and support supplier-related processes.

The agents can collaborate across their respective environments, subject to configured access permissions and governance.

This is an important development because it moves enterprise AI away from isolated agents toward a more connected ecosystem.

The future of enterprise AI will depend not only on intelligent agents but also on their ability to communicate and collaborate securely.

6. Personalized AI Experience Across Web, Desktop, Mobile, and Voice

Another interesting aspect of the Joule Work announcement is its cross-device experience.

SAP presented Joule Work as a redesigned experience accessible across multiple interaction channels:

  • Web.

  • Desktop.

  • Mobile.

  • Voice.

  • Apple CarPlay.

This reflects an important change in how employees expect to interact with enterprise applications.

Business users should not need to be sitting in front of a desktop computer to access enterprise intelligence.

For example, a manager travelling between business locations could interact with Joule through supported mobile or voice experiences to access information and stay connected with business activities.

SAP also highlighted the ability to create skills that work across desktop and web experiences, helping provide consistency across different interaction surfaces.

The broader vision is to make enterprise AI available wherever employees need it.

7. Business Context: Making Joule Work Understand Your Organization

An AI assistant can generate answers quickly, but enterprise decisions require more than general knowledge.

An organization has its own business processes, policies, customer relationships, financial rules, and operational dependencies.

For Joule Work to provide meaningful assistance, it needs access to the context that defines how the organization operates.

SAP is enhancing SAP Knowledge Graph capabilities to incorporate additional SAP and non-SAP data sources specific to each customer.

Users can query and explore customized enterprise data using natural language, helping ground AI responses in their own business information.

Consider a sales manager asking:

"Which customers have declining sales, outstanding payments, and high business risk?"

Answering this requires more than retrieving sales figures.

The system needs to connect customer profiles, sales history, invoices, payment information, and relevant business relationships.

By improving access to enterprise-specific knowledge, SAP is working toward making Joule Work more context-aware and relevant to individual organizations.

The real differentiator is not just AI intelligence. It is AI intelligence grounded in your business.

8. SAP Joule Work: What Makes This a Significant Change?

The evolution of Joule Work represents a fundamental shift in how employees interact with enterprise technology.

This is more than a new interface. It is a change in the relationship between employees, enterprise applications, and AI.

9. The Bigger Vision: From Application-Centric to Intent-Driven Enterprise

The most important takeaway from SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 is the shift toward an AI-native enterprise experience.

Traditionally, employees have been required to understand application navigation, identify the right transaction, retrieve information, and manually coordinate activities.

With Joule Work, SAP is moving toward a model where employees can express their intent and AI helps coordinate the required activities.

The vision can be summarized in five steps:

The Joule Work experience

  1. Express business intent

    The employee describes the desired business outcome using natural language.

  2. Understand and plan

    Joule interprets the request and plans the activities needed.

  3. Coordinate assistants and agents

    Relevant assistants and agents are orchestrated across business domains.

  4. Connect enterprise systems

    SAP and supported third-party applications provide the required information and capabilities.

  5. Support business execution

    The coordinated workflow helps deliver the requested outcome within configured governance and permissions.

This is the direction SAP is taking toward the autonomous enterprise, where AI becomes an integral part of how business work is performed.

Conclusion: The Future of Work Is Not About More Applications. It Is About Better Outcomes.

SAP Joule Work represents an exciting evolution in enterprise AI.

The announcements at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 demonstrate SAP's ambition to transform the employee experience through a unified AI interface, intelligent agent orchestration, connected applications, personalized interactions, and enterprise-specific business context.

What makes this transformation particularly interesting is the move away from application-centric working toward intent-driven execution.

Employees should be able to focus on what needs to be achieved rather than spending time figuring out where information resides or which application to use.

With Joule Work, SAP is working toward a future where conversations become workflows, agents become collaborators, and enterprise applications become part of a connected AI experience.

The next generation of enterprise productivity will not be measured by how many applications employees use, but by how effectively they achieve business outcomes.

And that is what makes SAP Joule Work an important development in the journey toward the autonomous enterprise.

entry.title: SAP BTP Job Scheduling Service — Introducing New Job Type: Destination Job
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Job Scheduling Service on SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP) is the backbone of automated, time-driven workloads for cloud-native applications. Whether you need to trigger a nightly data sync, execute a recurring business process, or run a long-running background task — the service has you covered, across both the Cloud Foundry and Kyma runtimes, through a unified REST API and a web-based dashboard.

Historically, the service offered two job types:

  • HTTP Jobs — Invoke an application's action endpoint over HTTP (synchronously or asynchronously) within your Cloud Foundry space or Kyma namespace.
  • CF Task Jobs — Execute long-running Cloud Foundry tasks bound to a specific application in your CF space.

These two types are powerful within their respective boundaries. But enterprise workloads rarely live in a single space or namespace. Applications on SAP BTP frequently need to integrate with external systems — partner APIs, SAP cloud services in other subaccounts, on-premise backends, or internet-reachable third-party services. Until now, bridging that gap required writing intermediary proxy code just to relay a scheduled call outward.

That changes with the new Destination Job type.

What Is a Destination Job?

A Destination Job is a new job type in SAP Job Scheduling Service that allows you to call external applications — applications that are not part of your Cloud Foundry space or Kyma namespace — on a defined schedule.

Instead of pointing to an internal action endpoint URL, a Destination Job resolves its target through the SAP Destination service. This means the entire connectivity and authentication chain — URL resolution, token handling, proxy routing, certificate management — is offloaded to a managed BTP service that you almost certainly already use across your landscape.

Important: Destination Jobs support only destinations created via the SAP Destination service. Ad hoc URLs or hardcoded endpoints are not supported for this job type.

For a full overview of how to create and manage destinations, refer to the official SAP documentation: Managing Destinations on the SAP Help Portal.

Why Destination Jobs Matter

Modern enterprise architectures on SAP BTP are composed of multiple runtimes, subaccounts, and external systems. Consider these common scenarios:

  • A Cloud Foundry application needs to trigger a scheduled process in an SAP S/4HANA Cloud system.
  • A Kyma microservice must push periodic data to a third-party SaaS platform via REST API.
  • An automated job needs to call a remote integration flow running in SAP Integration Suite.
  • A scheduled process must invoke a backend in a different CF space or subaccount using a destination configured at subaccount level.

In all these cases, the target application is outside the scheduler's own runtime boundary. Previously, you'd need to build and maintain an intermediate service to receive the job trigger, resolve the destination, and relay the call. With Destination Jobs, the scheduler handles this natively — no proxy layer, no extra middleware.

How It Works

Destination Jobs integrate directly with the SAP Destination service. Here is the execution flow:

SAP Job Scheduling Service
         │
         │  (at scheduled time)
         ▼
SAP Destination Service
  ├── Resolves destination by name
  ├── Retrieves target URL
  ├── Performs authentication flow
  │     (OAuth2, Basic, Client Cert, etc.)
  └── Returns connection details
         │
         ▼
External Application / API
  (outside CF space / Kyma namespace)
  1. At the scheduled time, the Job Scheduling Service picks up the Destination Job.
  2. It calls the SAP Destination service and resolves the named destination to a target URL and authentication token.
  3. It then invokes the external application using the resolved connection.
  4. Execution status and run logs are captured back in the Job Scheduling Service dashboard.

Prerequisites

Before creating a Destination Job, ensure the following are in place:

RequirementDetails
SAP Job Scheduling Service instanceA service instance must exist in your BTP subaccount (Cloud Foundry or Kyma).
SAP Destination service instanceA Destination service instance must be created and accessible in the same subaccount.
Destination configuredAt least one destination must be created and configured via the SAP Destination service in the BTP cockpit.
Dashboard accessYou must have the SpaceDeveloper role (CF) or SAP_Job_Scheduling_Service_Admin role (Kyma) to access the dashboard.
Target application reachableThe external application must be reachable from BTP using the configured destination (internet, Private Link, or on-premise via Connectivity service).

Supported Destination Methods

Destination Jobs support only destinations created via the SAP Destination service. The SAP Destination service offers several methods to connect to external systems, each suited to different security and connectivity requirements. You can choose from these when setting up your destination in the BTP cockpit:

MethodUse Case
No AuthenticationPublic APIs or internal endpoints that require no credentials.
Basic AuthenticationUsername and password-protected services on the internet or on-premise.
Client Certificate AuthenticationMutual TLS (mTLS) — internet or Private Link endpoints requiring a certificate.
OAuth2 Client CredentialsService-to-service integrations with OAuth2-protected APIs (most common for scheduled workloads).
OAuth2 JWT BearerToken exchange flows where the calling service asserts an identity via JWT.
OAuth2 SAML Bearer AssertionSAML-based trust flows, commonly used with SAP systems.
OAuth2 User Token ExchangeUser context propagation within the same tenant.
Principal PropagationOn-premise connectivity with user identity forwarding (requires SAP Connectivity service).

For a complete list and configuration guidance, see Managing Destinations on the SAP Help Portal.

How to Create a Destination Job via the Dashboard

The SAP Job Scheduling Service dashboard is your central hub for managing all job types, including the new Destination Job. Here is a step-by-step walkthrough.

Step 1 — Open the Job Scheduling Service Dashboard

You can access the dashboard in two ways:

Via SAP BTP Cockpit:

  1. Log in to the SAP BTP Cockpit.
  2. Navigate to your Subaccount → Services → Instances and Subscriptions.
  3. Locate your Job Scheduling Service instance.
  4. Click View Dashboard from the Actions menu.

Via Service Bindings (CF):

  1. In your Cloud Foundry space, go to Service Instances.
  2. Find the Job Scheduling Service instance.
  3. Click the (Open Dashboard) icon in the Actions column.

Note: You must have the SpaceDeveloper role (CF) or the SAP_Job_Scheduling_Service_Admin role (Kyma) to access and manage jobs in the dashboard.

Step 2 — Navigate to Jobs

Once in the dashboard:

  1. In the left navigation area, choose Jobs.
  2. The Jobs overview lists all existing jobs, along with their type, status, and schedule details.
  3. Choose Create Job to begin creating your new Destination Job.

Step 3 — Configure the Destination Job

In the Create Job dialog, fill in the following fields:

FieldDescription
NameA unique, descriptive name for your job (e.g., sync-external-crm-data).
Job TypeSelect Destination Job from the available job types.
Destination NameEnter the name of the destination as it appears in the SAP Destination service (case-sensitive).
HTTP MethodSelect the HTTP method the job should use when calling the external application (e.g., GET, POST, PUT).
Path / EndpointOptionally specify a path relative to the destination's base URL (e.g., /api/v1/sync).
PayloadFor POST/PUT methods, provide the request body to send to the external application.
DescriptionA human-readable description of what the job does (optional but recommended).
ActiveToggle to activate the job immediately upon creation.

Tip: Ensure the destination name you enter exactly matches the name defined in the SAP Destination service cockpit — including capitalisation and special characters.

Step 4 — Add a Schedule

A job without a schedule does not run. After creating the job:

  1. Open the newly created job from the Jobs list.
  2. Navigate to the Schedules tab.
  3. Choose Create Schedule.
  4. Configure your schedule using one of the supported formats:
FormatExampleDescription
Cron expression0 2 * * *Runs at 02:00 every day
Recurring intervalPT1H (ISO 8601)Runs every 1 hour
Specific date/time2026-12-01T06:00:00ZOne-time execution
Human-readable repeat1 hourSimple recurring format
  1. Optionally, set a Start Date/Time and an End Date/Time to bound the schedule window.
  2. Choose Create to save the schedule.

Step 5 — Monitor Execution and Logs

Once your Destination Job is active and scheduled:

  1. In the dashboard, open the job and go to the Logs or Run Logs section.
  2. Each schedule execution is recorded with its status (SUCCESS, FAILED, RUNNING) and timestamp.
  3. Detailed logs help diagnose connectivity issues, authentication failures, or unexpected responses from the external application.

Tip: For production workloads, consider enabling SAP Cloud ALM integration from the dashboard's Actions menu to monitor your Destination Job's health alongside other operational data in SAP Cloud ALM. This integration was introduced in May 2025.

All Three Job Types — A Complete Comparison

FeatureHTTP JobCF Task JobDestination Job
TargetInternal app endpoint (URL)CF task in bound appExternal app via SAP Destination
ScopeWithin CF space / Kyma namespaceWithin CF space onlyOutside CF space / Kyma namespace
Target resolutionDirect URLCF APISAP Destination service
Execution modeSync or asyncAlways asyncHTTP (via Destination)
Created via REST APIYesNo (dashboard only)Yes
Destination service requiredNoNoYes
Authentication handled byApplication codeCF runtimeDestination service
Best forInternal API automationLong-running background tasksCross-boundary external integrations

Use Cases

Here are real-world scenarios where Destination Jobs deliver the most value:

1. Cross-Subaccount Integration Trigger a scheduled process in a service deployed in a different BTP subaccount, using a subaccount-level destination that points to it.

2. Periodic S/4HANA Cloud Sync Schedule a daily job to call an SAP S/4HANA Cloud OData service — authenticated via OAuth2 SAML Bearer — to push or pull business data without maintaining a proxy application.

3. Third-Party API Automation Call an external SaaS platform's REST API on a schedule (e.g., a marketing automation tool or a logistics tracking API), using OAuth2 Client Credentials for service-to-service authentication.

4. SAP Integration Suite Triggering Trigger an iFlow in SAP Integration Suite at a scheduled time, using a destination configured with the relevant endpoint and credentials.

5. On-Premise Backend Calls Invoke an on-premise backend system (via SAP Connectivity service and Cloud Connector) at a defined interval — the destination handles proxy routing transparently.

Best Practices

  • Name destinations clearly — Use descriptive, environment-specific names (e.g., s4hana-prod-odata, crm-api-staging) so jobs are easy to audit.
  • Prefer OAuth2 Client Credentials for automated, unattended service-to-service calls — it is the most suitable authentication type for scheduled workloads.
  • Test your destination first — Use the Check Connection feature in the BTP Destination cockpit to validate the destination before creating the job.
  • Use recurring schedules over one-time schedules — SAP Job Scheduling Service deletes one-time schedules that have not run within the last 30 days (as of May 2025).
  • Enable SAP Cloud ALM monitoring — For business-critical Destination Jobs, activate Cloud ALM integration to get visibility into execution health.
  • Secure your payloads — Avoid embedding sensitive data in job payloads. Use destination properties and authentication flows to handle credentials securely.

Conclusion

The Destination Job is a focused, well-placed addition to the SAP Job Scheduling Service toolkit. It removes the architectural workaround that developers previously relied on — building proxy endpoints just to bridge the gap between a scheduler and an external application — and replaces it with a first-class, destination-aware job type.

By leveraging the SAP Destination service, Destination Jobs inherit a proven, secure, and centrally managed connectivity layer. The result is simpler architecture, less code to maintain, and a scheduling capability that is genuinely fit for today's multi-system, cross-boundary enterprise landscapes.

If your team already manages destinations in BTP for other integration scenarios, onboarding to Destination Jobs is straightforward. The same destination you use elsewhere in your application can now also power a scheduled job — no duplicate configuration, no new connectivity setup.

Try it out today via the Job Scheduling Service dashboard or the REST API, and let your scheduled workloads reach as far as your architecture demands.

entry.title: Re: how to display the reference infor field in FI12.
entry.content:
Hi Tokey,

Your two screenshots helped, because I think the difference is the country, not the release. In S4 company code 1010 has a bank in CN, and in ECC company code SCS has a bank in SG. I read the logic in my S/4HANA 2023 and 2020 labs. I don't have an ECC system, so please compare there.

The field is T012K-REFZL (Reference Information), on screen 0002 of SAPLFHBANKC. The screen has it as invisible by default, in modification group 3 with value 002. In PBO, module MODIFY_0002 calls FI_BL_SCREEN_GROUP_MOD with the ISO country of the company code, and that function reads table TFIBLSCREEN. The field only appears if there is an entry for that country with PROGNAME = SAPLFHBANKC, SGRNO = 3 and SGRVL = 002. SCRUSE 3 means input field.

In both labs the table has this entry for 33 countries. CN is one of them and SG is not, which matches what you see. Your screenshots also come from different view clusters (VC_T012N in S4, VC_T012 in ECC), but both use view V_T012K and the same screen, so I don't think that is the reason.

So I would check in ECC:

  • The country of company code SCS (T001-LAND1) and its ISO code (T005-INTCA). The rule looks at the company code, not at the bank country.
  • TFIBLSCREEN in SE16 with PROGNAME = SAPLFHBANKC. If the company code is in SG and there is no line for SG, SGRNO 3, SGRVL 002, that is the cause.

To show the field you would need that line. In my labs the table has a maintenance view, V_TFIBLSCREEN, but it is a system table with delivery class S, so a line of your own is a change on SAP's content, and I would look for an SAP note for your country first.

What I measured: the screen and its flags, the code of MODIFY_0002 and FI_BL_SCREEN_GROUP_MOD, and the content of TFIBLSCREEN, identical in both labs. I didn't run FI12 live with a company code or add any line, so test it in a sandbox first.

entry.title: Re: Historical Reporting for Processed Customer Payment A...
entry.content:
Hi Harshi,

Before building a report on your staging table, I would check what the standard already keeps. Payment advices live in AVIK (header) and AVIP (items), and leaving the posting screen doesn't have to mean they are gone. This is what I read in my S/4HANA 2023 lab:

  • Reporting: RFAVIS30 "Payment Advice Overview (Header and Item Data)" reads AVIK and AVIP directly, RFAVIS10 is the shorter overview, and FBE3 displays one advice. For a report of your own, I_PaymentAdvice and I_PaymentAdviceItem are released (C1).
  • Line detail: AVIP has the reference (XBLNR), the reason codes (RSTGN and the external one, RESTG) and the item text (SGTXT), and AVIR keeps the sub-items with their own reasons, so the deductions and the line-by-line breakdown you miss in FBL5N should be there while the advice exists.
  • Retention: RFAVIS20 "Payment Advice Notes: Reorganization" deletes old advices, with two rules in its code. An advice with AVIK-XKEEP ("Hold Payment Advice in the System?") is skipped, unless the checkbox for held advices is set on the selection screen with a retention period. All the others wait for the days in T053G-ANZTG ("Days Until Deletion"), per advice type, in view V_T053G. In my labs types 01 to 08 have 10 days and type 09 has 0.

So here is the quick test: take a posted advice number and look for it in AVIK with SE16. If the row is there, RFAVIS30 can already give you the history. Then check if RFAVIS20 runs as a job and with which variant, and raise the days in T053G or use the hold flag to keep them longer. If the row is gone right after posting, your staging table is probably the right source after all.

What I measured: the code of RFAVIS20, the fields of AVIK, AVIP and T053G, the release state of the views, and the delivered T053G values. I didn't trace the clearing step itself, so I can't say what it does to the advice in your flow, and my lab has no advice data to try it, so please test it in a sandbox first.

Hi,

From what I read in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, yes, nothing in this API depends on a purchase order. There is just one point to check, about what you mean by remittance.

  • The key of an item is company code, account type, account, advice number and item. The account type can be D (customer), K (vendor), S (G/L account) or G (business partner FI-CA). A non-PO invoice has an FI document, so the item can point to it with AccountingDocument and FiscalYear, or with DocumentReferenceID, which is the invoice reference (XBLNR).
  • The only field that looks like a PO is PurchasingDocReferenceByCust. It comes from AVIP-BSTNK, labelled "Customer Reference", so I read it as a reference text and not as a link to a purchase order.
  • The service can write: A_PaymentAdvice has create, update and delete enabled, and A_PaymentAdvice and A_PaymentAdviceItem are released for remote use (C2). The same lab also has a newer RAP service, API_PAYMENTADVICE, on top of A_PaymentAdvice_2 and A_PaymentAdviceItem_2, with the same item fields.

The point to check: this API stores payment advice notes (tables AVIK and AVIP), which are used later to clear open items. As I read it, it doesn't pay the invoice or send anything to the vendor. So if by payment remittance you mean an incoming advice that helps to clear, it fits. If you mean the remittance advice you send after a payment run, that is another flow, in the payment program. If you tell me which side you are on, I can look at that part too.

What I measured: the DDL sources of A_PaymentAdvice, A_PaymentAdviceItem and I_PaymentAdviceItem, the behavior of A_PaymentAdvice_2, the values of domain KOART_AV and the release states. I didn't call the API or post a clearing with it, so please try it in a sandbox first.

entry.title: Re: Issue with Customer Numbering Series in SAP HANA
entry.content:
Hi Surya,

No gaps while you keep creating, and a gap when you come back days later: that pattern is what number range buffering usually looks like, so I would check this before looking for an error in the account group. The system reserves a packet of numbers in the memory of the application server, and what is left of that packet is lost when the instance restarts or the buffer is reset.

I can see the same thing in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, in business partner number range 01:

  • Object BU_PARTNER has main memory buffering with 10 numbers in the buffer, and object DEBITOR has it with 5 (table TNRO). My S/4HANA 2020 lab has the same values.
  • BUT000 has 23 jumps in that range. For example, partner 102 was created on 28 Dec 2024 and the next one is 111, on 30 Jan 2025. Partner 332 was created on 19 Nov 2025 and the next one is 341, on 20 Oct 2026. In all 23 jumps the next partner was created on a later day and its number ends in 1, which is the first number of the next packet of 10.
  • NRIV is at 350 while the last partner is 342, so the rest of the current packet is already reserved.

To check it on your side:

  1. In view V_TBD001, see if your grouping has Same Numbers set. If it does, the customer number comes from the BP number and the object to look at is BU_PARTNER. If not, it is DEBITOR.
  2. In SNRO, look at the fields Buffering and No. of Numbers in Buffer for that object. SM56 shows the number range buffer.
  3. List the last numbers with their creation date (CRDAT in BUT000, ERDAT in KNA1). If each jump lands on the start of a packet and is never bigger than the buffer, compare those dates with the restarts of PRD. With more than one application server, each one holds its own packet, so numbers can also come out of order.

Then it is a business decision. Numbers lost this way don't come back, but nothing is wrong with the customers you created, so if nobody needs a series without gaps, I would leave it as it is. If it is really required, the setting to change is Buffering = No buffering in SNRO. Two things to weigh first: both objects belong to SAP (DEBITOR in package FBD, BU_PARTNER in S_BUPA_GENERAL) and the setting is per object, so it counts for all your groups and is a change to a standard object; and every new number then goes to NRIV, so parallel creation can wait on the lock, which you would notice most in mass loads. Please try it outside PRD first.

What I measured: TNRO and NRIV in both labs, the view and its Same Numbers field, and the BUT000 numbers and dates in the 2023 lab. What I didn't do: I didn't compare those dates with the restarts of my lab, I didn't change the buffering or watch a restart, and I can't see your PRD, so for your case this is the likely cause and not a proven one. If you share a few numbers with their dates, I'm happy to look at them with you.

entry.title: Re: Planned depreciation not calculated/recorded when per...
entry.content:
Hi Giuseppe,

I'm not from SAP, just another member here, but I looked at your screenshots and I think the case is narrower than "low value". In both assets the book value is exactly 0.01, left by Z33, X93 and X91 on 01.01.2026, and one cent can't be split:

  • WEET, remaining life 7 years and 1 month: 0.01 over 85 periods is about 0.00012 per period, or 0.0014 per year.
  • WE3B at 3.5%: 3.5% of 0.01 is 0.00035 per year.

Neither reaches half a cent. In my S/4HANA 2023 lab, class CL_FAA_EE sends the calculated depreciation through _ROUND_DEPRECIATION and _ROUND_VALUE, which round to the currency decimals, so the result is 0.00. I read that as expected behavior and not as an error of the run. I couldn't find a note for this exact case in the public pages I can search.

Why OAYO reaches other assets: its table T093B has only company code and depreciation area as key, and the newer table FAAC_CMP_DA0 only adds the ledger. So in customizing the rounding is the same for every asset in the area.

A standard way to limit it: BAdI FAA_DC_CUSTOMER has the method CHANGE_ROUNDING ("Change Rounding Specifications"). The depreciation calculation calls it with a handle that has the asset data, and the method can change what is rounded (A = amount, V = net value), the rounding method (0 = arithmetic, 1 = up, 2 = down), the places and the decimals. SAP's sample CL_EXM_IM_FAA_DC_CUSTOMER filters by asset class 2000, company code 1000 and area 01. In your case the class alone would still catch normal assets, so I would filter by asset number (it is in the handle, in ms_asset_data-s_asset_key), for example from a small custom table with the assets of that operation, and apply there the values that solved the cent in your OAYO test. The method also exists in my S/4HANA 2020 lab, so I would expect it in your release, but please check it in SE18.

Two simpler checks before any code. In AW01N, move the fiscal year forward to the last year of the WEET asset: I would expect the remaining life to leave the whole cent in that year, and if so, only the percentage assets need something. And if they are few, a manual unplanned depreciation (ABAA) of 0.01 may be enough.

I only read the code and the table definitions. I didn't implement the BAdI, run a depreciation or create an asset like yours, so the last year and the effect on periods already posted are not proven. Please try it in a sandbox with one asset in scope and one out of scope, and compare the planned values in AW01N before and after. And if you get a note from SAP on this, I would be glad to know too.

entry.title: Re: PO version text for version 0
entry.content:
Hi,

From what I read in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, customizing alone can't do it, but the standard code has a place for this text, so a small enhancement should be enough.

  • Customizing: table T16CA (by document category, type and purchasing organization) holds Version Management Active, the field status of Reason, Short Text, Requester, External Number and Posting Date, and Version 0 Completed, the flag you set. There is no field for a default text, so that flag only closes version 0 as it is.
  • The place in the code: when a new version is created, method if_revision_manager_dcm~create_item (include LMEDCMMF01) copies a proposal into it. The comment there gives the examples MEKR, MEKL "or BAdI calls". You set the proposal with function MEDCMM_SET_PROPOSAL, structure EREV_PROPOSAL, which has the text (TXZ01), the reason (RSCOD), requester, external number, posting date and version completed (REVOK). The text is copied only if the Short Text field status in T16CA is optional or required.
  • Where to call it for ME59N: program RM06BB30 calls BAdI MM_PUR_AUTOPO_PREPROCESS, method PREPROCESS_REQUISITIONS, and it creates the POs with CL_PO_HEADER_HANDLE_MM. MEDCMM_REFRESH doesn't clear the proposal (that line is commented out), so as I read it one call serves all the POs of the run.

One trap: the automatic completion of version 0 has the condition "g_proposal is initial", with the comment "not if set via proposal". So once you set a proposal, your Version 0 Completed flag is ignored, and you must also pass REVOK = X in the proposal, otherwise version 0 stays open.

If you create POs by API instead, BAPI_PO_CREATE1 has the parameter VERSIONS with DESCRIPTION, REASON and COMPLETED, but I didn't see ME59N using this BAPI.

The BAdI and the function also exist in my S/4HANA 2020 lab. I only read the code and the tables: I didn't run ME59N or implement the BAdI, and I see no release state for the function, so treat it as a classic extension. Please test it in a sandbox, and check that the proposal doesn't reach other documents, because it stays in memory.

entry.title: Re: Flexible Workflow for Condition Contract – Approval H...
entry.content:
Hi Laura,

From what I read in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, I don't see a place where the standard keeps the approver once the workflow history is gone, so you will need to choose how to keep it. First, why you only see SAP_WFRT: the release doesn't happen in the approver's session. Class CL_WCB_CC_WF_FLEX_RUNTIME receives the final result in its result callback and, for RELEASED, calls WCB_CONDITION_CONTRACT_RELEASE, so the workflow runtime makes the status change. And in the 90 fields of WCOCOH I found no approver field.

I see three ways, from the least work to the most:

  1. Archive instead of delete. Archiving object WORKITEM (WORKITEM_WRI writes, WORKITEM_DEL deletes) keeps the work items out of the database, and RSWWARCR and RSWWARCP are its read programs. There is no code in this one, so I would take it to the owner of the policy first.
  2. Copy before the cleanup. A small report, scheduled before the deletion job, reads the work items of task TS02000679 "Decide on Release of Condition Contract" in SWWWIHEAD, where WI_AAGENT is the last agent, takes the contract from SWW_WI2OBJ (TYPEID BUS2235, INSTID) and saves them in your own table.
  3. Capture at the decision. SAP already uses BAdI /IWWRK/BADI_WF_BEFORE_UPD_IB for this contract: implementation WCB_IMPL_CC_WF_RELEASE_ACTIONS, class CL_WCB_IMPL_CC_WF_REL_ACTIONS, gets the work item details and the decision key and finds the contract number. Your own implementation could save these with the user. Two cautions: it runs before the decision is saved, so a decision that fails later would stay in your table, and it belongs to the inbox runtime, so as I read it, it doesn't cover decisions made elsewhere. SAP also has the work item exit CL_WCB_CC_WF_DECISION_EXIT for the same check, which is why I suspect there is a second path.

The classes and the BAdI interface also exist in my S/4HANA 2020 lab. I only read the code and the tables. My lab has no work items for that task, so I didn't approve a contract, run the archiving or implement anything, and I can't say how option 2 looks with several approval steps. As I understand it, each step is a work item, so you would get one row per approver, but please confirm that in a sandbox.
