entry.title: CDS View Extensions in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: Architecture, Tools, and What Matters
entry.content:
***Applies to: SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2023 FPS01 and later. CDS extension mechanics apply from S/4HANA 1909 onwards; the Joule connectivity described here requires 2023 FPS01+***

Part 1 of 2 | Series: Your SAP S/4HANA Data Model Is Your AI Strategy

Picture this scenario. As part of an SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition transformation project, your company has just enabled Joule on the SAP Fiori Launchpad. The demo has gone well. The finance lead is keen. Within the first week she asks: "Can Joule tell me the margin by our internal product tier classification?"

The answer is it cannot. Not because Joule can’t surface it, but because your product tier classification has been sitting in a Z-table since the SAP ERP days and was never added to any CDS view. From where Joule sits, that data does not exist. The same gap is blocking the OData API your integration team wants to expose. The same gap is blocking the SAC model your analytics team is trying to build.

One missing CDS extension. Three blocked workstreams.

That is the argument for getting CDS extensions right. Not one platform. All of them.

Supporting customers in my role as SAP S/4HANA RIG solution architect, I see this pattern on almost every transformation engagement and it rarely arrives alone.

Now picture the procurement lead sends a different request that same week: "Can we get planned delivery time into the purchasing analytics dashboard?"  This one looks identical from the outside - another field Joule and SAC cannot see - but the cause is different. Planned delivery time already exists in SAP’s database. It is standard SAP data that simply has not been promoted to any released CDS view. No Z-table, no custom logic, but the fix is not the same either.

Two situations. Same symptom. Different cause. Different path. Let's work through both.

The SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition Context

In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, SAP manages the HANA database, application server, and OS layers on hyperscaler or SAP’s own infrastructure. You own the application configuration, the transport landscape, and the extension estate. That split matters more than it sounds.

The release rhythm is: a base release every two years (S/4HANA 2023, 2025, 2027), Feature Pack Stacks every six months within a base release, delivering incremental innovations, and Support Pack Stacks after mainstream cutover, carrying only fixes. Mainstream maintenance runs seven years per base release. Under RISE with SAP, SAP executes the upgrade; you own the readiness work and the cutover decision.

In practice, that means upgrade preparation sits on your plate, and the quality of your extension determines how much of that preparation is analysis versus remediation.

Here is what upgrade readiness actually means for extensions. SAP runs the Software Update Manager (SUM) against your development system. As part of that process, ABAP activation checks run against every object in the customer namespace. Any extension that references an internal SAP object that has changed, which can be a view structure, a table field, or an association cardinality, will throw an activation error. Those errors block the transport chain. You cannot promote to QA or production until every activation failure in the development system is resolved, re-tested and re-transported. On a program with 50–100 custom extension objects, even three or four failures, you can add hours to days to a cutover window that is usually already tight.

The mechanism that prevents this is the C1 release contract. When SAP marks a CDS view as C1-released, it is a formal architectural commitment: the view's interface, its field names, types, and association signatures, will not change in ways that break downstream consumers. If your extension targets a C1-released view using EXTEND VIEW ENTITY, SAP owns the upgrade compatibility. If you've extended an unreleased view, used a Z-copy of a standard view, or written Classic ABAP that reads internal table structures directly, there is no contract and no guarantee. The ABAP Test Cockpit (ATC) will tell you how exposed you are; running it against your extension estate before each FPS is not optional, it's the earliest point at which you find out what needs to be fixed.

On-premise teams have exactly the same structural problem. The difference is that on-premise teams control the upgrade schedule and can defer it. In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, that deferral option is limited; you stay current, or you fall out of mainstream maintenance. That is why the extension quality conversation that on-premise programs have been able to postpone tends to arrive earlier and more urgently for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition.

The Extensibility Stack: Where CDS Extensions Fit

SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition supports the full SAP extensibility portfolio. Understanding where CDS extensions sit within it matters before choosing your approach.

CDS view extensions, written as EXTEND VIEW ENTITY in ADT, sit in the Developer In-App tier. When targeting C1-released views, they are Level A: ABAP Cloud compliant and fully upgrade-safe.

One practical note specific to SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: in a system configured with the ABAP Cloud language version, the compiler will reject references to unreleased objects. This is not a warning; it is a build failure. That enforcement mechanism is one of the more useful guardrails the platform provides.

Clean Core, Release Contracts, and Upgrade Safety

The A–D Classification

SAP's Clean Core framework maps to something concrete: whether your extension object activates cleanly after an upgrade without manual intervention.

Level

What it means

CDS extensions land here when...

A

ABAP Cloud compliant, released objects only

Targeting C1/C0-released views with EXTEND VIEW ENTITY

B

Stable interfaces, not fully cloud-ready

Extending views with partial release contracts

C

References internal SAP artifacts

Using unreleased views or internal objects

D

Direct modification of SAP standard

Not appropriate


Level A costs upfront discipline — checking release contracts, following the bottom-up propagation pattern, using the right syntax. That investment is front-loaded: a few extra steps at build time that translate into a quieter, lower-risk upgrade cycle. Level C and D extensions tend to surface at upgrade time as activation failures that need to be resolved before cutover.

Release Contracts

Before extending any CDS view, check its release contract. This is the formal binding between SAP and you on interface stability.

Contract

Name

What it means

What it enables

C0

Extend

Stability at defined extension points only. Has two visibility scopes: Use in Key User Apps or Use in Cloud Development — or both

CDS view extensions, append structures, BAdIs. Use in Key User Apps scope makes the view available in Custom Fields & Logic (F1481) and SCFD_REGISTRY tools

C1

Use System-Internally

Stable public interface guaranteed for use within the ABAP system. SAP will not change the interface in ways that break downstream consumers after an upgrade

Using the view as a data source in custom ABAP development within the same system

C2

Use as Remote API

Stable public interface guaranteed for use outside the ABAP system

Consuming the view via OData, remote function calls, or external API clients

No contract / internal

Unreleased

No stability guarantee — SAP can change or remove the object without notice

Nothing. Referencing these places your extension at Level C or D in the clean core classification

In ADT, open the target view and navigate to the API State tab. A C1 or C0 contract means SAP has committed to not changing the interface in ways that break extensions. @vdm.lifecycle.contract.type: #PUBLIC_LOCAL_API is a further contract type indicating a stable, released public interface — also safe to build on.

The Virtual Data Model: Your Extension Target

SAP's Virtual Data Model is a semantic stack with deliberate layering:The rule that matters most: extend at the lowest layer where the data lives and let it propagate up. If you only extend the consumption view, the OData service bound to the interface view won't see your field. If you extend the interface view, every consumer up the stack including OData, SAC, Fiori, Joule inherits it automatically.

You can see this layering live in the Fiori View Browser app (F2170). Search for I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01, which is the view used in the code examples throughout this post. The results list shows its VDM View Type as Basic, confirming this is the interface layer: above the physical database, below the consumption views. This is the layer your extension targets.

In ADT, the view type is declared explicitly on every SAP-delivered VDM view via @vdm.viewType: #BASIC, #COMPOSITE, or #CONSUMPTION. This annotation drives behaviour in SAC, Embedded Analytics, and Fiori Elements, and tells you which layer you're working with before writing a single line of extension code.

Never extend P_* (private) views: no release contract, subject to change by SAP without notice.

Two Kinds of Data Gap

Two distinct situations produce the same symptom - a consumer that cannot find the data it needs. Diagnosing which one you are dealing with determines your path.

Gap 1: A Standard SAP Field Not Yet Exposed

The field exists in a standard SAP table, such as EKPO, MARA, LFA1, VBAP, but no released CDS view has ever selected it. This is more common than expected. SAP has exposed the majority of high-traffic fields through released views, but the long tail of table columns that matter to specific business scenarios is substantial.

First step: confirm with Alternative Search in View Browser (F2170)

Before concluding a field is unavailable, use the Alternative Search function. Open the View Browser (F2170), switch to the Alternative Search tab, and enter the table name and field name. This searches across all released CDS views for any that read that field from that table — including views you would not have found by name.

If no results carry the Released status, even if internal views reference the field, it is not accessible through any stable CDS interface. PLIFZ returns 86 views in this search shown above. None are Released. From Joule, SAC, or any OData client, this field does not exist.

Once confirmed, three paths forward in clean core preference order:

Option 1 — Key User path (cleanest)

Check whether the field's business context is available in the Custom Fields app (F1481). If it is, add the field as a key user extension. SAP handles CDS propagation and OData registration automatically. No developer code required and the result is Level A clean core.

Option 2 — Wrapper view (developer path)

If the key user path is not available, build a minimal custom CDS view that reads the fields directly from the SAP standard table, then extend the released interface view with an association to this wrapper. The wrapper reads unreleased SAP table structures — Level C in the clean core model. It works and can be made stable, but it carries an upgrade risk if SAP restructures the underlying table. Document it explicitly, add the base table to your Simplification List checks before each FPS and track it as technical debt until SAP delivers a clean release.

Note on ABAP Cloud mode: In an SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition system configured with ABAP Cloud language version, direct access to unreleased tables like EKPO will be rejected at compile time. Option 1 or Option 3 are the only supported paths in that configuration.

-- Wrapper view: reads unreleased SAP table directly (Level C in clean core)
-- Only build this after confirming the field is not already exposed
-- using Alternative Search in View Browser (F2170)

Option 3 — Request SAP to release the field

Submit a feature request via . SAP reviews these and adds fields to released CDS views based on demand. The right long-term resolution when the field is strategically important, and the wrapper approach introduces unacceptable upgrade risk.

Gap 2: Custom Business Data

If the data was never part of SAP's standard model — it lives in a Z-table carried over from an SAP ERP landscape, or was built fresh during the current implementation — Alternative Search will return nothing by design. The field isn't missing from SAP's views; it simply doesn't exist in SAP's data model at all.

The resolution here is the developer extension pattern: build a CDS view on your custom table, then extend the relevant SAP interface view with an association to it. The data stays in your Z-table, the CDS layer becomes the bridge. Every consumer above, including OData, SAC, Fiori, Joule, gains access through that association. The worked example later in this post walks through this .

The Extension Toolkit: Key User and Developer Paths

Once you know what gap you are filling, you have two supported extension paths in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. They are deliberately separate and cannot directly consume each other's outputs.

The Key User Lane

Custom Fields app (F1481) — No ABAP, no ADT. Create custom fields, extend data sources, and implement custom logic within a form-based UI. When a view is available as a data source in this app, the platform handles CDS propagation, OData registration, and Fiori field placement automatically. The result is Level A clean core.

Custom CDS Views app (F1866A) — A guided SAP Fiori application for building analytical and external API views without code. Select a scenario (Analytical Cube, Standard CDS View, or External API), choose from released SAP data sources, define joins through a form, and activate. The system generates the CDS source.

Use it when: your requirement is analytical reporting or a simple external API, all data sources are released SAP views, and the logic fits what the form can express.

Hard limits: you cannot use it if you need association-based views also exposed as OData (mutually exclusive in the app) or if your data source is a Z-table. Custom CDS Views created here carry no C1 release contract. In ABAP Cloud development (the standard for Level A clean core), they cannot be consumed as a data source. Classic ABAP can access them, but at the cost of coupling key user and developer extensibility layers, which is worth documenting as a dependency. The reverse also holds: views extended through ADT cannot be used as data sources in the app.

The Developer Lane

Code-first, full CDS DDL language, managed in your own development project in ADT. This is the path for anything the app can't handle: extending existing SAP views bottom-up through the full VDM stack, working with RAP business objects, or building the data model foundation that feeds a Joule skill.

The template you select in the ADT New Data Definition wizard depends on the base view type:

  • define view → select Extend View template → syntax: extend view Base with ExtensionName { }
  • define view entity → select Extend View Entity template → syntax: extend view entity Base with { }

Most standard SAP VDM views in older S/4HANA releases use the classic define view syntax. Newer RAP-based views use define view entity. Always check the first line of the target view in ADT — the two syntaxes are not interchangeable.

Before You Extend: Three Checks

Whether you're coming from Gap 1 or Gap 2, these checks apply to the target view before writing extension code.

  1. API State in ADT: C1, C0, or #PUBLIC_LOCAL_API contract. @Metadata.allowExtensions: true indicates direct metadata extension support. Registration in SCFD_REGISTRY (check 2) is the complementary signal for field-list extensions via EXTEND VIEW ENTITY.

  1. SCFD_REGISTRY: Views registered here are explicitly designed for extension. The Custom Fields app (F1481) can also drive extensions to them.

  1. Structural blockers — Views using GROUP BY, UNION, or UNION ALL cannot have their select list extended. Check @AbapCatalog.viewEnhancementCategory. If it's #NONE, build a custom view on top instead.

The Core Pattern: Extending for Custom Business Data

The following section works through a complete extension for the Gap 2 scenario: custom business data in a Z-table that needs to be visible to Joule, SAC, and a custom OData service.

Choosing your method

Before writing a line of code, understand which of the three developer-side methods applies. They produce different results and are not interchangeable.

Method

How

OData / Fiori handled

Best for

Key User — Custom Fields (F1481)

Fiori UI, no ABAP

Automatically — standard UI, OData, and Fiori field placement wired up by the platform

Simple fields in released views, where standard Fiori UI placement is the goal

Developer — Extension Include

ADT: append to an SAP-provided E_* include structure; extend the view to expose it

Partially — field is in the view; OData exposure still needs a custom Service Binding

Views with a pre-registered extension include (_Extension association visible in ADT); cleanest developer path when available

Developer — Z-table + Extend View

ADT: custom Z-table, basic CDS view on it, extend the standard view with a new association

Manually — you create a Service Definition and Service Binding in ADT

Full developer control; enrichment from external data sources or data with no counterpart in SAP's model

How to choose in practice:

  • Open the Custom Fields app (F1481). If the view appears in the data source list as Released, use the key user path.
  • Open the view in ADT. If you see a pre-defined _Extension association pointing to an E_* include view, SAP has pre-wired an extension point. Add an append to the include structure and extend the view to expose the field, and no Z-table is needed.
  • If neither applies, the view is not in the Custom Fields app (F1481) and has no pre-wired extension include, use the Z-table approach below.

What the worked example uses: the Z-table + Extend View path. This is the most general approach and the one most commonly needed for custom enrichment scenarios. It requires the most manual steps but gives you complete control over the data model.

Worked Example

A manufacturing company needs to add a sustainability certification reference (ZZ_SUSTAIN_CERT_REF) to purchase order items so it is available for Datasphere replication, custom analytical queries and downstream applications built on the extended CDS view.

Step 1, Create the custom extension table. Create a transparent Z-table (ZPOITEM_SUST) with MANDT, EBELN (PurchaseOrder), and EBELP (PurchaseOrderItem) as key fields, plus ZZ_SUSTAIN_CERT_REF as the payload field. Create a basic CDS view (ZI_POItemSustain) on top of it. This table is the data store for the extension; the CDS view makes it joinable from the standard view layer.

Step 2, Extend the interface view:

@AbapCatalog.sqlViewAppendName: 'ZEXPOITEMSUST'
@EndUserText.label: 'Extend PO Item — Sustainability Cert'

extend view I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01
  with ZEX_I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01
  association [0..1] to ZI_POItemSustain as _ZPOItemSustain
    on  $projection.PurchaseOrder     = _ZPOItemSustain.PurchaseOrder
    and $projection.PurchaseOrderItem = _ZPOItemSustain.PurchaseOrderItem
{
  -- Expose the field from the extension table
  _ZPOItemSustain.ZZ_SustainCertRef,

  -- Expose the association so path expressions work downstream
  _ZPOItemSustain
}

Syntax note: I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01 uses the classic define view syntax, so its extension uses extend view Base with ExtensionName { } with a mandatory @AbapCatalog.sqlViewAppendName annotation. Select the Extend View template in ADT. Use $projection.FieldName in association ON conditions to qualify base view fields and avoid ambiguity errors.

Step 3a, Verify at the CDS layer:

With ZEX_I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01 activated, ZZ_SustainCertRef is now part of the extended I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01 view. Verify by opening the view in ADT and pressing F8 (Data Preview). The column should appear alongside standard PO item fields. Add a row to ZPOITEM_SUST for a real PO item first so you have a non-null value to confirm.

Step 3b, Expose via a custom OData service:

The standard SAP purchase order API (API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV) has an explicit contract and does not inherit CDS view extensions. To expose ZZ_SustainCertRef via OData, you need a custom service definition and binding.

Create and Activate the Service Definition

  • Name: ZSD_POITEMSUSTAIN

@EndUserText.label: 'PO Item Sustainability Extension'
define service ZSD_POITEMSUSTAIN {
  expose I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01 as PurchaseOrderItem;
}

Create, Activate and Publish the Service Binding

  • Name: ZSB_POITEMSUSTAIN
  • Binding Type: OData V4 – Web API
  • Service Definition: ZSD_POITEMSUSTAIN

The editor shows the service URL once published.

Append /$metadata to the service URL and search for ZZ_SustainCertRef. It will appear as a property on the PurchaseOrderItem entity type. Query the entity set for a PO item that has a row in ZPOITEM_SUST to confirm the value is returned.

Joule: The custom OData service published here is the data source for a Joule skill. Register ZSB_POITEMSUSTAIN as a BTP destination, point a Joule skill at that endpoint, and Joule can surface ZZ_SustainCertRef in natural language responses alongside standard PO item data. The CDS extension is the foundation, one field added at the interface layer, surfaced through every consumer that reads from the service.

What this extension does not do automatically: expose the field in SAP's standard A2X API (API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV) or in the standard Fiori UI. For Fiori UI visibility, the same extend view pattern applies to the item-level consumption view that backs your target app.  Identify it in View Browser (F2170) and add an equivalent extension with @UI annotations. For standard API exposure, the supported path is the Custom Fields app (F1481), which handles the service registration as part of the key user extensibility flow.

Performance Considerations

A few principles worth stating upfront, before they become debugging sessions later.

Use associations, not joins, for optional enrichment data. An association resolves only when a consumer navigates it. A join executes unconditionally on every query. For custom enrichment tables — classification data, custom attributes, legacy reference data — associations are almost always the right choice. A poorly placed join on I_JournalEntryItem (backed by ACDOCA with hundreds of millions of rows in production) can have a significant impact on query response time.

Declare cardinality accurately. [0..1] vs [1..1] on an association is not cosmetic. Incorrect cardinality can cause the query optimiser to generate multiply-joining plans, producing duplicate rows or forcing outer joins where inner joins would suffice.

Avoid calculated fields in ON and WHERE clauses. Computed expressions in join conditions prevent HANA from pushing predicates to the storage layer. The result is a scan instead of a seek.

Validate with ST05 and ADT Dependency Analyser after activation. What runs in 200ms on a sandbox with 50,000 rows may behave differently on a production system with 800 million. Test with realistic data volumes before promoting to quality.

Pre-Flight Checklist Before You Extend

Before writing a line of code on any SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition extension:

  • ☐ Base view has C1, C0, or #PUBLIC_LOCAL_API contract, verified in ADT API State tab
  • ☐ View registered in SCFD_REGISTRY, or @Metadata.allowExtensions: true present on the base view
  • ☐ Enhancement category is not #NONE
  • ☐ No GROUP BY or UNION in the base view
  • ☐ Gap type confirmed: standard SAP field (Alt Search in View Browser first) or custom data
  • ☐ Bottom-up propagation plan mapped out, every layer from DB to consumption
  • ☐ Extension object created in ABAP Cloud software component (compiler enforces release contract compliance)
  • ☐ Associations used for optional data, no unconditional joins on high-volume views
  • ☐ Cardinality declared accurately on all associations
  • ☐ Naming convention followed: ZEX_I_*, ZEX_C_*, ZEX_Q_*
  • ☐ Transport dependency order documented, extension activates after base view

Governance Checklist Per Extension

For architect sign-off on any extension going to quality:

  • ☐ Release contract confirmed (ADT + SCFD_REGISTRY)
  • ☐ ABAP Cloud software component used, compiler passes without released-object violations
  • ☐ All VDM layers propagated bottom-up, confirmed end-to-end in the Fiori app and OData service
  • ☐ Performance reviewed, ST05 trace run on production-scale data
  • ☐ Simplification List checked, base objects not deprecated in target release
  • ☐ Downstream consumers inventoried: Fiori apps, SAC, Datasphere, OData clients, Joule skills if applicable
  • ☐ If OData exposure needed: service definition and binding created, BTP destination configured
  • ☐ Transport landscape validated, correct promotion order in dev → QA → prod

Part 2 picks up here: six situations you are likely to encounter on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition projects, with the exact technical detail of what goes wrong and why, and the full architecture chain from CDS extension to working Joule skill, end to end.

entry.title: Scalable and Reliable Large-Volume Data Synchronization Using SAP Integration Suite Pipeline Orchest
entry.content:
Introduction

Organisations frequently need to synchronise large volumes of business data, such as master data, transactional records, financial information, and order data, between enterprise systems. Such integrations must be designed to process high data volumes efficiently while ensuring reliability, recover-ability, and minimal impact on source and target system performance.

This article describes an orchestration-based synchronisation framework built using SAP Integration Suite. The solution leverages JMS queues, pipeline integration flows, and parallel processing principles to transfer large datasets reliably and efficiently between source and target systems.

In this use case, the source system contains master data records that need to be synchronised with a target system without impacting operational performance.

The source system exposes APIs that provide the following capabilities:

  1. Retrieve the total number of records available for synchronisation.
  2. Retrieve a specific set of records based on page number and page size for a given date range.

By utilising SAP Integration Suite as the orchestration layer, large datasets can be split into manageable batches and processed independently, enabling scalability, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilisation.

High-Level Solution Architecture

Process Flow Overview

  1. Initiation: Scheduled Trigger

The synchronisation process begins with a scheduler that triggers the workflow at predefined intervals based on business requirements.

Once triggered, a message is placed into an initial JMS queue. This design provides decoupling between process stages and ensures message persistence. In the event of temporary connectivity failures or unexpected processing issues, the message remains available for automatic retry and reprocessing.

Key Benefits

  • Scheduled execution
  • Reliable message persistence
  • Automatic recovery from transient failures
  • Decoupled processing architecture

  1. Planning: Determine Processing Scope and Create Jobs

After the workflow is initiated, the planning phase identifies the volume of data that must be synchronised.

During this step:

  • The source system API is invoked to retrieve the total record count.
  • The total number of pages is calculated based on the configured page size.
  • Required processing parameters are generated, including page number and page size.
  • A separate job message is created for each page of records.
  • All generated jobs are placed into a JMS queue for execution.

This approach converts a large synchronisation activity into multiple smaller and independently executable jobs.

Example

If:

  • Total Records = 1,000,000
  • Page Size = 10,000

Then:

  • Total Jobs = 100

Each job is responsible for processing one page of records.

Key Benefits

  • Workload distribution
  • Improved scalability
  • Independent processing of batches
  • Better system resource management 

  1. Execute Jobs from the Queue

Once jobs are available in the JMS queue, the execution flow starts processing them immediately.

For each job:

  • The corresponding message is consumed from the JMS queue.
  • The source API is called using the assigned page number and page size.
  • The requested batch of records is retrieved.

Using JMS as the processing backbone provides resilience against temporary API failures. If connectivity issues occur during execution, the message remains available for retry according to the configured retry mechanism.

Key Benefits

  • Reliable batch processing
  • Automatic retries
  • Failure isolation
  • Parallel execution capability

  1. Retrieve Records and Deliver to the Target System

After successfully retrieving a batch of records from the source system, the data is forwarded to the target system through the SAP Integration Suite pipeline framework.

The processing utilises:

  • Pipeline Generic Step 06 – Outbound Processing
  • Pipeline Generic Step 08 – XI Outbound Processing

Step 06 provides built-in retry capabilities and reliability handling. If message delivery fails during Step 08 processing, the framework automatically retries transmission based on the configured retry settings.

This layered design ensures guaranteed delivery while maintaining high throughput for large volumes of data.

Key Benefits

  • Reliable target system delivery
  • Automatic retry handling
  • Reduced data loss risk
  • Standardised outbound processing framework

Solution Benefits

The proposed orchestration pattern provides several advantages for enterprise-scale integrations:

Scalability

Large datasets are divided into smaller processing units, enabling efficient handling of millions of records.

Performance Optimisation

Paginated data retrieval minimises load on the source system while reducing memory consumption within the integration platform.

Reliability

JMS-based processing ensures message persistence and recovery from temporary failures.

Parallel Processing

Multiple jobs can be processed simultaneously, significantly reducing overall synchronisation time.

Re-usability

The framework can be reused for synchronising:

  • Master Data
  • Order Data
  • Financial Data
  • Customer Data
  • Product Data
  • Transactional Records

Monitoring and Support

Each job represents an individual processing unit, simplifying operational monitoring, troubleshooting, and error recovery.

Conclusion

By combining SAP Integration Suite Pipeline Flows, JMS queues, and pagination-based processing, organisations can build a scale able and resilient synchronisation framework capable of handling high-volume data transfers efficiently. The solution minimises dependency on source system performance, provides built-in recovery mechanisms, supports parallel processing, and ensures reliable delivery to downstream applications.

This orchestration pattern serves as a reusable enterprise integration blueprint for synchronising large-scale master data, transactional data, financial records, and other business-critical information across heterogeneous systems.

entry.title: SAP-RPT vs. SAP-RPT-TS: A Beginner's Guide
entry.content:
At SAP TechEd on October 27, 2026, SAP announced SAP-RPT-TS, a new model for forecasting business numbers over time. It is generally available today in SAP HANA Cloud and SAP AI Core (SAP TechEd news guide).

It joins SAP-RPT, SAP's tabular foundation model, whose current version is SAP-RPT-1.6. The names are similar, but the two models do different jobs. This guide explains the difference in a few minutes, no data-science background needed.

The short answer

SAP-RPT fills in a missing value in a table. SAP-RPT-TS predicts how a number will move over time. Both are pretrained, so you get answers without first training a model on your own data.

Figure 1. SAP-RPT fills in a label (classification) or a number (regression) for each record. SAP-RPT-TS continues a number over time (forecasting). Illustrative data.

SAP-RPT: filling in the blanks

You send rows where the answer is known plus rows where it is missing, and SAP-RPT fills the blanks in one call, with no retraining. Each row stands on its own, so row order doesn't matter.

  • SAP-RPT-1 (SAP TechEd 2025): classification and regression. An open-source version, sap-rpt-1-oss, is on Hugging Face.
  • SAP-RPT-1.6: the current version, with a standard variant optimized for low latency and a large variant optimized for prediction quality (model documentation).
  • SAP-RPT-2 (announced at SAP TechEd 2026): adds anomaly detection, embeddings and multi-table processing; general availability planned for Q1 2027 (SAP TechEd news guide).

Typical uses: late-delivery or late-payment risk, a customer's risk class, days until an invoice is paid.

SAP-RPT-TS: looking ahead in time

You send the history of a number, for example three years of weekly sales, and SAP-RPT-TS returns the coming weeks. No training is needed; this is called zero-shot forecasting (SAP Community).

  • Patterns from the sequence. It learns recurring patterns, such as trends and daily or weekly cycles. Events such as holidays or promotions can be supplied as covariates: extra data known for the past or in advance, so the model can use their timing explicitly.
  • A range, not just one number. For example: most likely 1,200 units next week, probably 1,000 to 1,450. Check how often the range held on your own history before using it to set safety stock.
  • Key facts. About 28 million parameters, so it runs on standard CPUs. Forecasts up to 1,024 steps ahead, across tens of thousands of series at once. Available in SAP HANA Cloud and SAP AI Core as sap-rpt-ts; planned for SAP IBP for Demand in Q1 2027 (SAP Community).

Typical uses: weekly demand per product, cash flow, call-center volumes and energy use.

Side by side

 

SAP-RPT

SAP-RPT-TS

What it reads

A table of separate records

A number recorded over time

Does row order matter?

No

Yes, it is the whole point

What you get back

A label or a number per row; regression results can include an interval

Future values, with a likely range at a level you choose

Example question

Will this order ship late?

How much will we sell next quarter?

Can one model do both? We tested it

Partly. SAP-RPT can forecast once you turn time into ordinary columns, which makes it a regression problem. SAP-RPT-TS skips that step. We tested both on the same job: forecast the next 24 hours of electricity demand in Victoria, Australia, for 319 days of 2014, each time from the same 1,024 hours (about six weeks) of history (Monash Electricity Demand dataset).

Inputs used in this experiment. SAP-RPT-TS received only the demand history, with no additional covariates. For SAP-RPT-1.6, we derived four features from the same history and its timestamps: hour of day, day of week, and demand at the same hour one day and one week earlier. Neither model received external inputs such as weather or electricity prices. SAP-RPT-TS supports additional covariates, but their effect was not tested here.

Figure 2. The same 1,024 hours of history: a sequence for SAP-RPT-TS, a table with four time columns for SAP-RPT-1.6. Values in GW.

Figure 3. Left: a day with typical errors for both models. Right: average error over 319 days; demand averaged about 4.6 GW.

  • SAP-RPT-TS was more accurate. Its average error was 24% lower, and it won on 245 of 319 days, in every month and at every hour of the day.
  • Check the ranges. 81.5% of actual values fell inside SAP-RPT-TS's 80% range overall, but only 61–68% from noon to 5 p.m., when demand is hardest to predict.
  • Holidays were hard for both; neither model was told about them.
  • Cost. Estimate consumption for your own workload with the SAP AI Core cost calculator. Actual costs depend on input size and commercial terms.

Important Note: one region, one year, no weather data, and the standard SAP-RPT-1.6 rather than the large version. Overlap with either model's pretraining data was not assessed. Treat this as an illustration, not a benchmark.

How to choose

Figure 4. Rule of thumb: if each record stands on its own, use SAP-RPT. If your question says "next week", "next quarter" or "the coming months", use SAP-RPT-TS.

The practical takeaway here is to choose the model for the question you need to answer.

Getting started

Both models are available today:

  • SAP-RPT: try it with your own CSV file in the free SAP-RPT playground, or call it through the generative AI hub in SAP AI Core (tutorial).
  • SAP-RPT-TS in SAP HANA Cloud: use the TSFM operator in the Predictive Analysis Library (PAL), on SAP HANA Cloud version 2026.28 (QRC 3/2026) or newer with NLP services enabled (SAP Community).
  • SAP-RPT-TS in SAP AI Core: call the model sap-rpt-ts through the generative AI hub, for example when your data lives outside SAP HANA Cloud (model documentation).

Note: Information about planned availability reflects SAP's current plans and may change at any time without notice. It is not a commitment to deliver any material, code or functionality.

entry.title: Protect Your iFlows: Add Access Control, OAuth 2.0, Spike Arrest and Quota with SAP API Management
entry.content:
The Scenario

I have an integration flow like this:
3rd Party ──► CPI (iFlow) ──► SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud

It works, but the third party calls CPI directly. That raises a few questions:

  • What if they send thousands of requests in a second?
  • What if someone calls from an unknown IP?
  • How do I give them their own credentials without sharing my CPI service key?
  • How do I limit how much they can use?

The answer is an API Management layer in front of CPI:
3rd Party ──► API Management ──► CPI (iFlow) ──► SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud
                                (policies here)

In this blog, I'll show you how to build it, step by step.

 What You'll Build
  • An API Provider that connects API Management to Cloud Integration
  • An API Proxy for your iFlow
  • Four policies: Access Control, OAuth 2.0, Spike Arrest, Quota
  • An API Product with a subscription (key and secret)
  • A working test in Postman or Bruno
Prerequisites
  • SAP Integration Suite with API Management enabled
  • A deployed iFlow (mine uses an HTTP sender adapter)
  • Two service keys in BTP. This is where people often get confused:

 

Service instance plan
Used for
apiCreating the API Provider (Step 1)
integration-flowThe proxy's backend authentication to trigger the iFlow (Step 2)

Important: For the API Provider, create the instance with plan api, not the iFlow plan. Then create a service key for it.

Step 1: Create the API Provider (Cloud Integration)

The API Provider tells API Management where your Cloud Integration tenant lives and how to authenticate against it.

  1. Open Integration Suite.
  2. Go to Configure → APIs → API Providers and click Create.

     

  3. Give your API Provider a Name.

     

  4. Go to the Connection tab and fill in:
Field
Value
TypeCloud Integration
HostHost from the url in your api plan service key
Port443
AuthenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials
Client ID / Client Secret / Token URLFrom the same api plan service key

Click Save.

Click Test Connection. You should see a success message.

🎉Your API Provider is ready!

Step 2: Create the API Proxy for Your iFlow
  1. In the same window, go to API Proxies and click Create.

Select Provider as the source and choose the API Provider you just created.
Click Discover.


Choose your iFlow from the list and click Next.

 

Set the backend Authentication Type to OAuth2ClientCredentials, then enter:

  • Client ID and Client Secret from the integration-flow plan service key
  • Token URL from the same service key

If Basic Authentication works better for you, you can use that instead. Then click Done.

  1. Adjust the Base Path if you like, since it becomes part of your endpoint.
  2. Choose the Service Type that matches your iFlow's sender adapter (in my case, HTTP).
  3. Leave everything else as is and click Create.

🎉Your API Proxy is created. Now let's make it smart.

Step 3: Meet the Policies

I'll apply four policies. Here's what each one does:

Policy
What it does
Think of it as
Access ControlAllows or denies requests based on the caller's IP addressA security guard checking the guest list
OAuth 2.0Verifies that the caller sends a valid access tokenAn ID badge check
Spike ArrestProtects the backend from sudden bursts of traffic by limiting the request rateA speed limiter
QuotaLimits the total number of calls a consumer can make in a time periodA monthly data plan

Spike Arrest vs. Quota: Spike Arrest protects APIs from sudden traffic spikes by smoothing short-term bursts (typically requests per second). Quota controls the total number of requests a consumer can make over a longer period (such as per hour, day, or month). Both policies complement each other and are often used together to provide effective traffic management.

How to open the policy editor
  1. Open your API Proxy and click Policies.

     

  2. Go to Proxy Endpoint → PreFlow in the left panel.
  3. On the right, you'll see the available policies. Find the one you need and click +.
  4. Give the policy a name and click Add.

You can reorder policies using the arrows in the upper right. I recommend this order: Access Control → OAuth 2.0 → Spike Arrest → Quota. Cheap checks go first, so bad traffic is rejected early.

 Policy 1: OAuth 2.0

Find OAuth v2.0 in the list, click +, name it, and click Add.

To use OAuth Policy, you also need a separate API proxy that generates the access token.

👉I've covered this in a separate blog: [link]. Please follow it first, then come back here.

Policy 2: Access Control

Find Access Control in the list, click +, and apply this policy:

 
<AccessControl xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt" async="true" continueOnError="false" enabled="true">
    <IPRules noRuleMatchAction="DENY">
        <MatchRule action="ALLOW">
            <!-- Load Balancer -->
            <SourceAddress mask="32">Paste IP Here</SourceAddress>
            <!-- App Servers -->
            <SourceAddress mask="32">Paste IP Here</SourceAddress>
        </MatchRule>
    </IPRules>
</AccessControl>​



How it works: Any IP not on the allow list is denied (noRuleMatchAction="DENY"). Replace the placeholders with your third party's real IPs.
Make sure enabled="true". With enabled="false", the policy exists but does nothing.
Which mask should I use?

The mask defines how many IPs a rule covers. Here is a cheat sheet.

Mask
Subnet mask
IPs covered
Example
Typical use
32255.255.255.2551203.0.113.25 onlyA single server, such as a third party's fixed IP. Best for most cases.
31255.255.255.2542.24 to .25Two paired servers
30255.255.255.2524.24 to .27A small group of servers
29255.255.255.2488.24 to .31A small server group
28255.255.255.24016.16 to .31A small office or datacenter block
27255.255.255.22432.0 to .31A medium block
26255.255.255.19264.0 to .63A larger block
25255.255.255.128128.0 to .127Half of a /24 network
24255.255.255.0256.0 to .255A whole company subnet
16255.255.0.065,536203.0.0.0 to 203.0.255.255A very large network. Usually too wide.
8255.0.0.016,777,216203.0.0.0 to 203.255.255.255Huge. Almost never appropriate.
00.0.0.0All IPsEverythingMatches everyone, so the rule becomes meaningless.
 Policy 3: Spike Arrest

Find Spike Arrest, click +, give it a name, and click Add.


<SpikeArrest async="true" continueOnError="false" enabled="true" xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Identifier ref="request.header.some-header-name"/>
    <MessageWeight ref="request.header.weight"/>
    <Rate>100ps</Rate>
    <UseEffectiveCount>true</UseEffectiveCount>
</SpikeArrest>

 

In plain words: This policy limits traffic to 100 requests per second per unique header value. The request's weight can reduce the allowed number further. This helps prevent backend overload and keeps your API stable.
Policy 4: Quota

Find Quota, click +, give it a name, and click Add.

<Quota async="false" continueOnError="false" enabled="true" type="calendar" xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Allow count="1000"/>
    <Interval>5</Interval>
    <Distributed>true</Distributed>
    <StartTime>2026-10-16 05:26:00</StartTime>
    <Synchronous>true</Synchronous>
    <TimeUnit>minute</TimeUnit>
</Quota>

In plain words: API consumers can make a maximum of 1000 calls in every 5-minute period.
Set StartTime to the current date and time, or a past one, so the counter starts immediately.
Save and Deploy

Click Update → Save → Deploy.

You now have a wrapper endpoint that you can share with third parties. 🎉
At this stage, you could already share the api plan service key credentials. But there's a cleaner, more professional way: API Products.

Step 4: Create an API Product

Products let you give each consumer their own key and secret, instead of sharing your service key.

  1. Go to Engage → Products and click Create.

     

  2. Enter a Name.
  3. Open the APIs tab and add the API proxies we created:
    • ✔️Your iFlow proxy
    • ✔️The Generate Token proxy (from the OAuth blog)

       

Click Publish.

Step 5: Subscribe in the Developer Hub
  1. Open the Developer Hub.

  1. Find your product and open it.

     

  2. From the Subscribe dropdown, select New subscription for application.

     

  3. Give the subscription a name and click Create.


You'll now see a Key and a Secret 🔑


You can give these to your third parties. Every product subscription gets its own credentials, so you can manage each consumer separately.

Using only an API key?
You can share just the key and ask the consumer to send it in the header as x-api-key. This works when you're using API key / Basic Authentication, and you may need to add a matching policy such as Verify API Key or Basic Authentication.

Since I'm using OAuth 2.0, the key and secret act as Client ID and Client Secret instead. Let's test that.

Step 6: Test with Postman / Bruno
  1. Create a new request with the API proxy endpoint URL of your iFlow.
  2. Under Auth, choose OAuth 2.0 and set Grant Type to Client Credentials.

Fill in the token details:

 

Field
Value
Access Token URLURL of the Generate Token proxy (see my OAuth blog: [link])
Client IDKey from the Developer Hub
Client SecretSecret from the Developer Hub

Click Generate Token, then use it to call your iFlow through the same API Management endpoint.

🎉Success!

Recap
  1. ✅Created an API Provider (api plan key)
  2. ✅Created an API Proxy for the iFlow (integration-flow plan key)
  3. ✅Applied OAuth 2.0, Access Control, Spike Arrest, and Quota
  4. ✅Bundled everything into a Product and subscribed
  5. ✅Tested with OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials
Over to You

Which policies do you use most in your projects? Have you tried others, such as JSON threat protection or response caching? Let me know in the comments!

If this helped you, give it a 👍 and follow for more SAP Integration Suite content.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 6: Transporting destinations
entry.content:
Part 6 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 5 role collections travelled through the Content Agent UI and needed an extra role and their own destination. Destinations are the opposite: they use the same road as integration packages and need almost no setup. The one thing to remember is what stays behind.

What travels and what stays behind

SAP's list of supported content types includes SAP Destination Service with the sub type Destination, and adds a clear note: "Content Agent service does not transport secrets and passwords." So the destination arrives in Central, but you enter its password or client secret there again yourself.

For the setup column, the same page says No setup needed. No new destination, no new node, no new route.

Step 1: Check the content type in Dev

Open the Content Agent UI in Dev and go to Content Types. SAP Destination Service should show Active. In my setup it already was.

Step 2: Pick the destination

Choose Export. On Add Content, search for the destination name and select the row with type Destination Service and sub type Destination.

Add Content in my setup: a role collection and a destination with the same name. The Type column tells them apart.

Step 3: Export to CTMS

On Export Details, the same choices as in Part 5: Export Mode SAP Cloud Transport Management, Create a New Transport Request, the source node and a description. I left Keep this Transport Request modifiable unchecked. Then Review and Export.

The log is worth a quick read: the MTAR is created, the request is created as not modifiable, and the last line confirms the content was transported to CTMS.

Export log in my setup (node name and process ID blurred).

Step 4: Import in Central

In CTMS, open the target node from Part 3, the one that uses CAS_on_target. The request lands in the same import queue as your integration packages. Select it, choose Import and confirm. In my setup the status changed to Succeeded.

Step 5: Finish the destination

  • In Central, go to Connectivity > Destinations. The destination is in the list.
  • Open it, enter the password or client secret again and save.
  • Test it from the application that uses it. For OAuth2ClientCredentials destinations, SAP Help notes that Check Connection is not a reliable test.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Two items with the same name. When I searched on Add Content, a role collection and a destination were both called "Test". Only the Type column showed which was which. Give destinations names you can recognise, and always check the type before you export.
  • Other requests were waiting in the queue. The target node already had older requests in status Initial. I selected only the destination request. CTMS then warned that importing single requests can lead to inconsistencies, because it does not check dependencies between requests. A destination on its own is fine. If an iFlow depends on it, import the destination first or together with the package.
  • No extra role this time. After Part 5 I expected another role problem. There was none: the destination import worked through the existing setup from Parts 3 and 4.

What comes next

Packages, role collections and destinations now all travel from Dev to Central. In Part 7, the last part, I put the whole series on one page: every service, destination and role in a single cheat sheet.

entry.title: Halloween, One Extra Zero and SAP's Tabular AI: Validating Campaign Orders with SAP-RPT-1.6
entry.content:
Halloween is behind us, and many retail chains are already placing their Christmas orders. SAP has announced the availability of SAP-RPT-1.6, tabular orchestration and the SAP-RPT playground API, and tabular AI had hands-on sessions at SAP TechEd 2026. Following SAP's latest announcement (SAP-RPT-1.6, Tabular Orchestration, and RPT Playground API: Now Available), I applied SAP-RPT-1.6 to a problem that comes back every year in retail: campaign orders.

One extra zero

In every major campaign (Halloween, Christmas, Diwali or any other peak buying season), the marketing team of a large retailer places thousands of order lines to refresh the look of hundreds of stores: banners, vinyls, displays, decorations. Each store has its own size, format and sales volume, and every line is filled in under time pressure.

At that volume, errors are inevitable: one extra zero (4 banners become 40), two swapped digits, units entered instead of packs, a hypermarket quantity in a neighbourhood store, or the same material ordered twice. None of them looks serious on the order screen. The trouble starts afterwards.

  • Goods receipts are posted automatically and have to be reversed.
  • Invoices are generated automatically and have to be rejected, and journal entries reconciled again.
  • It is not just marketing: IT has to step in to correct orders and cancel goods receipts.
  • If the error crosses a month-end close, as it does with Halloween, the reversals spill over into the following months.
  • The supplier produces and ships too much material, or a store is left without its campaign branding.

One extra zero multiplies the spend on that line by ten, ties up several teams for days and keeps the campaign's books open for weeks. Across thousands of lines and hundreds of stores, the error is no longer an anecdote: it is money lost, margin gone and teams firefighting at the busiest time of the year.

What I built

Drawing on my experience in the industry, I built a campaign order validator with a Fiori look and feel that checks the campaign order before it reaches SAP S/4HANA. It uses synthetic data, calls SAP-RPT-1.6 live through the SAP-RPT playground and creates the purchase orders in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. The flow has three steps:

Raw file uploaded by manager.

  1. Upload: the campaign manager uploads the file with every order line, one per store and material.
  2. Duplicates: a deterministic rule detects the same material ordered twice for the same store, and the user decides which line stays.
  3. Quantities: SAP-RPT receives, as context, a set of correct orders from previous campaigns together with each store's characteristics (format, floor area, sales, region). From that, it predicts how much each store should order of each material. If the quantity entered falls outside a reasonable range, the line is flagged and the user corrects it, or accepts it with a reason.

Every flagged line comes with its explanation: the expected quantity, the accepted range and the similar stores it was compared with. In the end, only validated lines become purchase orders in S/4HANA, through its standard API.

The results speak for themselves: in my tests with synthetic data, it caught 100 % of the quantity errors injected and every duplicate, with only 1 % false alarms.

Quantity check with the explanation of a flagged line

Purchase Order created from the app

 

Today this is an MVP: production would require work on governance, security, load testing and user experience. But the scenario is real, integrated end to end with S/4HANA, and it addresses a problem that consumer products and retail companies face in every campaign.

Why tabular AI

This scenario shows why tabular AI wins where other approaches fall short.

  • An LLM is not the right tool. General-purpose language models struggle to predict numbers from structured data: they mix up units and give different answers to the same question. I saw this first-hand in an earlier experiment comparing SAP-RPT-1 with several AI assistants.
  • A custom machine learning model is expensive. It has to be trained and, above all, retrained every time marketing trends, campaign materials or the store network change. For a seasonal process, that effort rarely pays off.
  • SAP-RPT learns on the spot. It receives examples of correct orders together with the lines to check, and predicts without any prior training. When the campaign changes, the examples change, not the model.

A problem that used to require a data science project is now solved with an API call.

Validate at the source

That is why the value goes beyond helping the person who fills in the order. Validating before the order reaches SAP avoids the downstream work in goods receipt, finance and IT, and protects the month-end close just when the campaign leaves the least room.

Closing

SAP's tabular AI now makes it possible to tackle everyday ERP problems that were never worth solving before, integrated with S/4HANA from day one. Retail campaigns are only the beginning: any mass upload with an "expected" volume, such as store replenishment, promotions or intercompany orders, follows the same pattern.

How many orders does your organisation correct after each campaign? Share it in the comments. And if you would like to see the demo or explore how to apply this to your processes, reach out: I will be happy to talk.
